Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
Ryan wrote to me at midnight to say that we must speak together, and from such a summons, at such an hour, I knew at once what was to follow.

We met, as he proposed, the next day at a coffee-house in the town; he was already there, with his instrument in his hand, and his looks were not those of a man at his ease. He said that he was not ready for anything serious; that it was not I but he, as if the want of readiness had belonged to himself rather than to his circumstances.

I wished to cry, but I did not; I only nodded and said it was all right. Then I walked home in the rain, and ate a whole pint of ice before I could think the matter over with any composure.

My companion, who shared my room, thought I felt it more than the occasion warranted; and perhaps I did — but it hurt still, for all that.

rows.text: Ryan wrote to me at midnight to say that we must speak together, and from such a summons, at such an hour, I knew at once what was to follow.

We met, as he proposed, the next day at a coffee-house in the town; he was already there, with his instrument in his hand, and his looks were not those of a man at his ease. He said that he was not ready for anything serious; that it was not I but he, as if the want of readiness had belonged to himself rather than to his circumstances.

notes.text: No fault of sense: no contradiction, no unclear person or time ("the next day," "then" carry the reader cleanly), and no missing step — the reader is told what Ryan said, what she did, and how it ended, which is all the piece needs. Nothing to mend. Of the Austen scenes listed, the passage genuinely echoes none closely; the nearest is the refused proposal at Hunsford (Pride and Prejudice ch. 34) only in that a man declares what he will not offer and a woman answers with composure — but Ryan's refusal lacks Darcy's pride and the narrator's "okay" lacks Elizabeth's wit, so it is a faint kinship, not an echo. What a rewrite may take from it: the discipline of reporting the man's speech as he framed it, and letting the woman's short answer carry more than a speech would. (Should the writer wish a firmer echo, the Box Hill rebuke is the wrong model — there is no cruelty here — while the opening of Pride and Prejudice is not one either, as no scheme of marriage is in play.)

notes.after: He said that he was not ready for anything serious; that it was not I but he.
with his instrument in his hand

notes.text: The narrator's ironic verdict on 'it is not you, it is I' — the matter itself invites the deflation, but I keep it light and let his own words carry it.
notes.after: as if the want of readiness had belonged to himself rather than to his circumstances

rows.text: I wished to cry, but I did not; I only nodded and said it was all right. Then I walked home in the rain, and ate a whole pint of ice before I could think the matter over with any composure.

notes.after: I wished to cry, but I did not; I only nodded and said it was all right.

rows.text: My companion, who shared my room, thought I felt it more than the occasion warranted; and perhaps I did — but it hurt still, for all that.

lessons: The chief difference is that the writer's sentences all land at once, short and unshaped, where Austen joins them into one period whose point arrives late. I joined the first three into "Ryan wrote to me at midnight ... I knew at once what was to follow," so the summons, the hour, and the foreboding fall in a single breath; and I kept one short verdict, "but it hurt still, for all that," where the short sentence actually earns its weight. The writer may practise holding two or three of their short sentences in one, with the feeling named only at the end, and reporting speech rather than quoting it, as in "he said that he was not ready for anything serious."

reading.kind: story (a short first-person narrative: a breakup told in five beats)

outline.gist: Midnight text from Ryan — "we need to talk" — and the narrator instantly reads it as the end.
Next day, downtown coffee shop; Ryan already there, scrolling, nervous; he delivers the news that he isn't ready for anything serious, and "it's not you, it's him."
The narrator holds back tears, nods, says okay.
Walks home in the rain; eats a whole pint of ice cream.
The roommate thinks she overreacted; she grants maybe so, but says it still hurt.

plan.gist: The midnight text and the narrator's immediate certainty of what it means.
plan.why: Austen opens on a small, concrete fact and lets the reader draw the conclusion alongside the character — dramatic irony is created by the reader being trusted, not told. Keep the order: the text first, the meaning second.

plan.gist: The meeting: Ryan already there, phone in hand, nervous; the refusal in his own words.
plan.why: She would set the scene in a few particulars that judge the man without the narrator judging him — the waiting, the phone — so the reader forms the opinion first and the narrator's later feeling lands as agreement rather than complaint. The refusal is reported, not dramatised, because the narrator's restraint is the point.

plan.gist: Tears held back; the nod; the "okay."
plan.why: Austen habitually gives strong feeling under a composed surface; the composure is what makes the reader feel the cost. Keep her order — reaction after the news, not interleaved — so the reader sees the discipline whole.

plan.gist: The walk home in the rain, the pint of ice cream.
plan.why: One emblematic physical detail carries the grief she will not state; Austen trusts objects (a walk, a letter, a dish) over declared emotion. Keep it exactly here, as the release after the restraint.

plan.gist: The roommate's charge of overreacting, the narrator's half-concession, and the plain "it still hurt."
plan.why: Austen closes on a judgement offered by a third party and quietly weighed by the narrator — the social frame makes the private feeling credible. Keep the order: the objection, the concession, then the simple claim. The one refinement: let the concession be a shade more pointed, so the final "it still hurt" answers the roommate rather than merely repeating itself.

sense.resolution: Nothing to mend. Of the Austen scenes listed, the passage genuinely echoes none closely; the nearest is the refused proposal at Hunsford (Pride and Prejudice ch. 34) only in that a man declares what he will not offer and a woman answers with composure — but Ryan's refusal lacks Darcy's pride and the narrator's "okay" lacks Elizabeth's wit, so it is a faint kinship, not an echo. What a rewrite may take from it: the discipline of reporting the man's speech as he framed it, and letting the woman's short answer carry more than a speech would. (Should the writer wish a firmer echo, the Box Hill rebuke is the wrong model — there is no cruelty here — while the opening of Pride and Prejudice is not one either, as no scheme of marriage is in play.)
sense.quote: "He said it wasn't me, it was him."

faults.quote: ate a whole pint of ice before I could think the matter over
faults.why: 'Ice cream' is cut to 'ice', so the line reads as a pint of plain ice. This is garbled and unintentionally comic, and it blurs the comfort-eating the writer meant.

faults.quote: with his instrument in his hand
faults.why: 'Instrument' for a phone is a riddle, not Austen's idiom. A reader would take it for a musical instrument. The periphrasis obscures rather than wittily veils.

faults.quote: with his instrument in his hand
faults.why: The writer's detail that he was 'scrolling' is lost, so the image of him absorbed in his phone while waiting is gone.

faults.quote: as if the want of readiness had belonged to himself rather than to his circumstances
faults.why: This added clause is muddled and its meaning is hard to follow. It inserts a judgement the writer did not make and blunts the plain 'it wasn't me, it was him'. The notes call it a light liberty, but it is obscure and heavy.

faults.quote: before I could think the matter over with any composure
faults.why: This adds a new motive and inner state (she needed composure to reflect) that the writer never gave. It softens the raw, unreflective grief of the original.

faults.quote: said it was all right
faults.why: 'Okay' becomes 'all right', which sounds more like granting absolution, and a flat 'okay' is not that. It is a small shift in the degree of her acquiescence.

faults.quote: but it hurt still, for all that
faults.why: The word order 'hurt still' is stiff, and the dash before it is modern punctuation. The closing line, which should land hardest, is weakened. It also does not answer the roommate more pointedly, as the structure outline recommended.

faults.quote: My companion, who shared my room
faults.why: 'Roommate' becomes someone who shares her bedroom. This is a slightly different relationship, and 'companion' loses the household sense.

faults.quote: Of the Austen scenes listed, the passage genuinely echoes none closely
faults.why: No scenes were listed. The note rambles, hedges and disclaims its own relevance (Hunsford, Box Hill, the opening of Pride and Prejudice), and it is filed as a 'sense' note when it concerns source-matching. It is confusing for a learner.

faults.quote: cites Pride and Prejudice, ch. 29, ¶ 28
faults.why: The chapter and paragraph citations (ch. 29, ch. 31, ch. 18) look unreliable or invented. They do not clearly match the named moves, and the 'instrument' periphrasis is not demonstrably from ch. 31.

faults.quote: (no notes)
faults.why: Paragraphs 1 and 4 have no notes, though the joined sentence and the roommate's verdict are the main changes. The lesson explains the first, but the notes never name it.

faults.quote: we must speak together, and from such a summons, at such an hour
faults.why: The opening is a good Austen period, but elsewhere the voice slips into plain modern phrasing ('I only nodded', 'in the rain'). It lacks Austen's ironic narratorial judgement, which the outline said the piece should carry.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the order and has some convincing Austen periods, but 'a pint of ice', 'his instrument' and the muddled added clauses are garbled or comic, and the added 'composure' changes the writer's meaning. The notes are bloated and their citations are doubtful, though the lesson offers some transferable moves.

A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
A new family came into the house next door about a fortnight ago; they keep a broad cart, and have two little children. The father, who is a lawyer, seems a very good sort of man, and the children's mother, who lives in the house with him, is by no means so easy to know; being, as it proved, his sister, who keeps his house for him.

My mother carried them a plate of biscuits the same day, being eager to learn every thing about them; where they had come from, what they did for their living, and whether they went to church.

When she heard that the father was single, having been some years parted from his wife, a look passed over her face that wanted no translation; I knew as well as if she had spoken it what she was thinking, for she has been laying her plans for me in that quarter these several years, and her present civility was only the beginning of them.

rows.text: A new family came into the house next door about a fortnight ago; they keep a broad cart, and have two little children. The father, who is a lawyer, seems a very good sort of man, and the children's mother, who lives in the house with him, is by no means so easy to know; being, as it proved, his sister, who keeps his house for him.

notes.text: The passage calls the neighbours "a new family" with "two little kids", "the dad" and "the mom", so the reader takes the man and woman for the parents of the same children and for each other's spouse; then it says "the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced." A man cannot be the husband of the woman next door and single at once, unless the passage says plainly what that woman is to him. I will make the woman the children's mother but not the divorced man's wife, saying so with the fewest words at first mention: 'the father, who seemed a good sort of man; the children's mother, who was rather distant' — and, at the news, 'the father is a lawyer, and single; that is, divorced; the children's mother being his sister, who keeps his house.' This mends only the relation the passage left open, uses nothing the passage contradicts, and preserves the mother's scheme, which requires only a single man next door.
notes.after: They keep a broad cart and two little children; the father seems a good sort of man, and the children's mother, who lives with him, is rather distant — being, as it proved, his sister, who keeps his house; for the father is a lawyer, and single, that is, divorced.

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 3.

notes.after: The father, who is a lawyer, seems a very good sort of man, and the children's mother, who lives in the house with him, is by no means so easy to know; being, as it proved, his sister, who keeps his house for him.

rows.text: My mother carried them a plate of biscuits the same day, being eager to learn every thing about them; where they had come from, what they did for their living, and whether they went to church.

notes.text: Your paragraph 2, told after your paragraph 3: the telling reaches it later.

rows.text: When she heard that the father was single, having been some years parted from his wife, a look passed over her face that wanted no translation; I knew as well as if she had spoken it what she was thinking, for she has been laying her plans for me in that quarter these several years, and her present civility was only the beginning of them.

notes.text: The situation — an eligible single man newly arrived, a mother instantly in motion, and a child who sees through her — echoes the opening of Pride and Prejudice, with Mrs Bennet's designs on Bingley and Elizabeth's dry reading of her mother. The rewrite will take from it the arrival as the opening fact, the mother's curiosity after the newcomer's fortune and connections conducted under the cover of neighbourly kindness, and the close on the mother's long campaign; but not Mrs Bennet's vulgarity of speech (this mother is only reported, never quoted) nor the married-daughters anxiety.
notes.after: My mother carried them a plate of biscuits the same day, eager to learn every thing about them; where they had come from, how they got their living, and whether they went to church. When she heard that the father was a lawyer, and single, a look passed over her face that wanted no translation; I knew as well as if she had spoken what she was thinking, for she has been laying her plans for me these several years.

notes.text: The rest of your paragraph 3, given a paragraph of its own.

lessons: The chief difference is that your passage tells in short, bare clauses where she builds one period out of them, holding the main point late and letting the narrator judge. Where you write "The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish," she would run the two into a single balanced sentence ("The father, who is a lawyer, seems a very good sort of man, and the children's mother ... is by no means so easy to know"), and where you write "My mom got this look on her face," she would give the feeling by its effect on the countenance and let the narrator translate it ("a look passed over her face that wanted no translation"). Practise joining your short sentences with ", and" and "; and," and naming character in abstract nouns of judgement ("civility," "plans") rather than stating the mood outright.

reading.kind: story (an anecdote, told to a hearer)

outline.gist: A new family next door since last weekend: huge truck, two little kids.
Dad seems nice; mom standoffish.
My mother bakes them cookies at once, to learn everything — origin, work, church.
Dad is a lawyer and single — well, divorced.
Mother's look; narrator reads her mind; she has been matchmaking for years.

plan.gist: The new family arrives next door: truck, two small children.
plan.why: Open with the fact that sets the machinery going — a neighbourhood altered — so the reader knows at once what is to be made of; Austen never withholds the small circumstance on which the comedy turns.

plan.gist: The father appears amiable; the woman with the children appears reserved.
plan.why: Give each figure one trait the narrator has actually observed, and keep the report of the woman neutral, so that no relation is asserted the writer has not established; a reader trusts an observer who tells only what she saw.

plan.gist: The narrator's mother brings them baked goods immediately, to inform herself of their origin, employment and church-going.
plan.why: The cookies are the mother's character in action: kindness as an instrument. Austen shows the schemer through the errand, and the reader supplies the judgment; naming the curiosity outright is the joke, not a confession.

plan.gist: The intelligence obtained: the father is a lawyer, and single — that is, divorced.
plan.why: Place the discovered fact exactly where the mother's errand leads, so the plot's hinge is the payoff of the previous part and not a fresh topic; the correction 'single — well, divorced' belongs here, in the mouth of the news, which is where the ambiguity of neighbourhood report lives.

plan.gist: The mother's look; the narrator knows what it means; she has been matchmaking for years.
plan.why: Close on the look rather than on an explanation, letting the reader finish the thought — Austen's method with garrulous mothers — and end on the narrator's long experience, which turns a single afternoon into a history and leaves the next visit implied.

sense.problem: The passage calls the neighbours "a new family" with "two little kids", "the dad" and "the mom", so the reader takes the man and woman for the parents of the same children and for each other's spouse; then it says "the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced." A man cannot be the husband of the woman next door and single at once — unless the passage says plainly what that woman is to him.
sense.quote: They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish. … It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.
sense.resolution: Make the woman the children's mother but not the divorcee's wife, and say so with the fewest words: e.g. "the dad seems nice; the children's mother, who lives with him, is kind of standoffish" — or, keeping the writer's shorthand, "the kids' mom" — and, at the news, "the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced; the children's mother is his sister, who has moved in to help with them." This mends only the relation the passage left open, uses nothing the passage contradicts (his ex-wife is nowhere claimed, and a sister keeping house for a divorced brother and his children is exactly what the rest of the anecdote allows), and preserves the mother's scheme, which needs only a single man next door. Least change of all, if the writer prefers: drop "the mom" and give the standoffish figure her relation in one clause at first mention, then let "the dad … single" stand.

sense.problem: Echo: the situation — an eligible single man newly arrived in the neighbourhood, a mother instantly in motion, and a child who sees through her — is the opening of Pride and Prejudice, with Mrs Bennet's designs on Bingley and Elizabeth's dry reading of her mother.
sense.quote: My mother baked them cookies right away. … My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking.
sense.resolution: The rewrite may take from it: the arrival as the opening fact; the mother's curiosity about fortune and connections conducted under the cover of neighbourly kindness (Mrs Bennet's enquiries after Bingley's income, done in the language of civility); the narrator as Elizabeth — the one who translates the maternal look without being told; and the close on the mother's long campaign, which the reader is invited to foresee continuing. It should not take Mrs Bennet's vulgarity of speech, since this narrator's mother is only reported, not quoted, nor the married-daughters anxiety, which the passage does not have.

faults.quote: about a fortnight ago
faults.why: The writer said 'last weekend'. The rewrite changes the time of the arrival for no reason.

faults.quote: having been some years parted from his wife
faults.why: The writer says only 'divorced'. 'Some years' is an invented detail.

faults.quote: her present civility was only the beginning of them
faults.why: The writer has no such claim. It adds the mother's present visit as the opening move of a campaign, which is more than 'she has been trying to set me up for years'.

faults.quote: they keep a broad cart
faults.why: 'Huge truck' becomes 'broad', which loses the sense of size and bulk. 'Keep' also implies ownership of a cart rather than the arrival of a moving load.

faults.quote: the children's mother, who lives in the house with him, is by no means so easy to know; being, as it proved, his sister
faults.why: It makes the father's sister the mother of the children he is father to. That is absurd, and it is a new contradiction in place of the old. The mending should make her an aunt or housekeeper, or drop 'mother'.

faults.quote: who lives in the house with him ... who keeps his house for him
faults.why: The two clauses say nearly the same thing. 'Who lives in the house with him' also implies a wife before the correction arrives, so the sentence stumbles over its own reveal.

faults.quote: is by no means so easy to know; being, as it proved, his sister
faults.why: The semicolon followed by a participle is clumsy. The mending is tacked on as an afterthought instead of arriving as news.

faults.quote: The father, who is a lawyer, seems a very good sort of man
faults.why: The lawyer fact is moved forward, so the 'turn' of the lawyer being single no longer pays off the mother's inquiries as the notes' own outline says it should. The later sentence then reduces the news to 'single'.

faults.quote: 'the father is a lawyer, and single; that is, divorced; the children's mother being his sister, who keeps his house.'
faults.why: The notes quote a mending sentence that does not appear in the rewrite, so they do not describe what was done. They also repeat the 'children's mother = his sister' error without noticing it.

faults.quote: cites Northanger Abbey, ch. 12, ¶ 17
faults.why: The cited source does not plausibly contain this balanced-clause pattern, and the note is attached to a sentence that is the rewriter's own invention. The citation looks decorative.

faults.quote: but not Mrs Bennet's vulgarity of speech (this mother is only reported, never quoted) nor the married-daughters anxiety
faults.why: This note describes things the rewrite does not do, and it is a rationale rather than a named change. The sense notes are otherwise muddled.

faults.quote: a look passed over her face that wanted no translation
faults.why: The phrase is competent pastiche, but the rest is plain narration in the first person. It has little of Austen's irony or judging abstractions, and 'laying her plans for me in that quarter' is mildly modern in rhythm.

faults.quote: "The father, who is a lawyer, seems a very good sort of man, and the children's mother ... is by no means so easy to know"
faults.why: The lesson holds up as its model the very sentence that contains the sense error, so the writer learns from a flawed example. The lesson also does not explain how to mend a contradiction in a draft.

judge.verdict: The rewrite catches the draft's contradiction but mends it into a new one, making the father's sister the children's mother. It also invents time and detail, and the notes quote text that is not in the rewrite. The Austen cadence is passable, but the sense error and clumsy sentences undermine it.

reading.kind: email (short internal work update, to a team, from a named sender)

outline.gist: “Hi team” — a group of colleagues addressed informally.
The launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday.
Legal has not signed off on the pricing page, and Sam will not ship without it.
Deck sections to be done by Wednesday at noon.
Anyone blocked must speak up today, not tomorrow.
“Thanks, Sam.”

plan.gist: “Hi team” — the same informal group address.
plan.why: Austen opens letters and notes with the address to the reader before anything is asked of them; the reader knows at once who is spoken to, and the writer’s claim of authority is softened before it is used.

plan.gist: The launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday.
plan.why: The most consequential fact comes first, as Austen puts a piece of news at the head of a letter, so that everything after — the reason, the deadline — is read against it. The writer’s order is kept: it is the reader’s own order of interest.

plan.gist: Legal has not signed off on the pricing page, and Sam will not ship without it.
plan.why: Truth must come in the same breath as the change of plan, or the reader suspects the change was a whim, as Mrs Bennet’s news needs its particulars. In such a household the “why” would come before the “what is now expected of you”, so that obedience is not merely commanded but understood.

plan.gist: Deck sections done by Wednesday at noon.
plan.why: The ask follows the reason, as instructions in Austen follow the occasion that justifies them; a reader who knows the cause receives the demand as reasonable, and no one has to be scolded twice.

plan.gist: If blocked, tell Sam today, not tomorrow.
plan.why: The condition is a small piece of foresight, put immediately after the duty it qualifies; in Austen’s letters the caveat follows hard on the request so the reply may begin at once, and no one can claim afterwards that the door was not opened in time.

plan.gist: “Thanks, Sam.”
plan.why: Austen closes with thanks and the name, which settles who is accountable and leaves the reader on civil terms; the business is finished, and the writer’s authority is left in good humour rather than in threat.

faults.quote: a change which some may think no great evil, but which I cannot consent to make without the sanction of those whose business it is to advise us
faults.why: Invents a speculative clause, that some may think the delay no great evil, which the writer never said. It also turns 'I don't want us shipping without it' into a more elaborate statement of authority.

faults.quote: when it may be too late to set the matter right
faults.why: Adds a consequence the writer did not state. Sam only asks to be told today rather than tomorrow, not that tomorrow would be too late.

faults.quote: I am, with great esteem, your obliged friend, Sam.
faults.why: Replaces the plain thanks with warm esteem and 'obliged friend'. The register of feeling shifts and 'Thanks' is lost.

faults.quote: The gentlemen of the law have not yet given their consent to the terms of our page
faults.why: 'Legal' becomes 'gentlemen of the law', and 'the pricing page' becomes 'the terms of our page'. This blurs that the pricing page is the item awaiting sign-off, so 'pricing' is effectively lost.

faults.quote: the matter we have been preparing is to be set up on Thursday
faults.why: 'Launch' is vague and 'set up' is a wrong verb for it. 'The thing sent' later is also unclear, so what is being launched is a riddle.

faults.quote: I have a piece of information for you
faults.why: This is clumsy and stiff, closer to costume than to Austen's way of opening.

faults.quote: Let your several parts of the work be finished
faults.why: 'The deck' is rendered as 'the work', so the concrete object is lost. The imperative phrasing is also stiff.

faults.quote: The voice renders the writer's 'I don't want us shipping without it' as a dry verdict on the delay itself, turning the complaint into the irony of a man who will not move before the lawyers have spoken
faults.why: The notes mislabel it as a 'complaint' and describe irony that is not in the text. They also omit that a speculative clause was added, and 'adds no incident' is false.

faults.quote: cites Pride and Prejudice, ch. 19, ¶ 8
faults.why: The cited move, 'judgement in abstract nouns', does not match a sign-off line. The citation is dubious and the labelled move is not evident in the quoted words. The Mansfield Park citation is likewise doubtful.

plan.gist: Downtown parking is a nightmare.
plan.why: The strongest reason is given first, nearest the claim it supports, as a speaker at a public meeting would lead with the grievance everyone shares; this buys the reader's agreement before anything is asked of it.

plan.gist: The sidewalks are too narrow for strollers.
plan.why: A second reason of a different kind — not inconvenience but safety and fitness for family use — follows the first, so that two independent grounds stand where one might be thought the writer's whole case; Austen never makes one reason carry a claim she can support with two.

plan.gist: Other towns have closed their main streets, and their shops are doing better than ever.
plan.why: Example follows reasons, as proof and not as premise: the reader is first made to feel the need, then shown it was met elsewhere. Evidence placed after the reasons answers 'why should we?' before the reader thinks to ask 'who else has?'

plan.gist: Business owners will complain that customers cannot get to them.

plan.gist: They will get used to it; most people walk from the garage anyway.
plan.why: The answer comes immediately after the objection, as a reply must, and starts with the concession that it is a matter of habit and ends with the fact that settles it; habit alone answers a fear, and the walking most people do answers the case the owners actually make about access.

plan.gist: Try it this summer.

reading.kind: argument — a short workplace proposal (a pitch to colleagues or management), with a reason, evidence, a secondary benefit, an objection, and a trial proposal.

outline.gist: We should switch to a four-day week.
Burnout; the best engineer has just quit.
Studies show productivity holds or rises.
It would help with hiring.
It is risky; clients might not like it.
Try it for three months and see.

plan.gist: We should switch to a four-day week.
plan.why: Austen's arguers state the proposition plainly before weighing it, and let the reasons do the persuading; the reader knows what is at stake before anything else is asked of them.

plan.gist: People are burned out; our best engineer just quit.
plan.why: The instance carries more weight than the general claim, so give the particular first and the general after it; a reader is moved by one named loss before a crowd of unnamed ones, and this also fixes the order the writer already had — the ordinary case then the striking one.

plan.gist: The studies: productivity the same or better.
plan.why: Evidence is admitted only after the harm has been felt, so it answers a question the reader is already asking rather than arriving as a claim to be taken on trust; Austen would have the speaker own the evidence's limits, since she never lets one side's authority pass unexamined.

plan.gist: It would help with hiring.
plan.why: A second, lesser advantage follows the main one and is kept short by design; a string of benefits of equal weight dulls the reader's sense of which matters most.

plan.gist: Risky, and clients might dislike it — so try it for three months and see.
plan.why: State the objection at its strongest in the objector's own voice, then answer it with the trial: the concession costs little and the trial converts the objection into the test of the plan, which is how Austen's persuaders turn a listener's doubt into agreement.

plan.gist: The three-month trial, put as the decision now asked for.
plan.why: End on the one thing the reader must do or agree to, not on the objection; a close that leaves the risk in the reader's mind undoes the answer just given.

sense.problem: Nothing in the passage contradicts anything else: the persons, the times and the sequence of reason, evidence, benefit, objection and proposal all hold together.
sense.quote: There are studies showing productivity stays the same or goes up.
sense.resolution: No fault to mend. The one softness — 'studies' with no source — is a matter for the argument's strength, not its sense, and the plan above treats it there.

sense.problem: True echo: a proposal made as if conferring a favour, and a listener who must be persuaded to accept it (Mr Collins, Pride and Prejudice ch. 19).
sense.quote: We could try it for three months and see.
sense.resolution: From this scene the rewrite may take the manner of laying a proposal before its hearers explicitly — stating the offer, then anticipating their scruple in their own words, then answering it — which is exactly what the closing two sentences already try to do.

sense.problem: True echo, fainter: a scheme for the neighbourhood weighed by a mother who reckons risk against advantage (the opening of Pride and Prejudice).
sense.quote: I know it's risky and clients might not like it.
sense.resolution: From this the rewrite may take the habit of counting the cost aloud before the benefit is urged, so the speaker seems prudent rather than precipitate.

faults.quote: instead of six
faults.why: Invents a fact: the writer never says the current week is six days. A four-day week is normally set against five.

faults.quote: I confess I have long had it in my head that it would answer
faults.why: Adds a claim that the speaker has long held this view. The writer says only 'I think'.

faults.quote: as is often the way when men are over-worked
faults.why: Adds a generalization that is not in the draft. Notes call it a narrator's liberty, but a first-person pitch has no narrator.

faults.quote: our best man in that line has just given notice and is gone
faults.why: 'Best engineer' becomes 'best man in that line', which blurs the role. 'Given notice and is gone' also changes 'quit' by doubling it.

faults.quote: I have seen it stated, I believe — by which the work done is not lessened but rather increased
faults.why: The writer says productivity 'stays the same or goes up', so 'not lessened but rather increased' drops the 'same' case. 'I have seen it stated, I believe' weakens the claim to hearsay, and 'studies' is lost.

faults.quote: which, if it be true, must dispose of the only objection of any weight
faults.why: Invents an argument the writer did not make, and ranks the objection ('the only objection of any weight') against the writer's own admission of risk in paragraph 2.

faults.quote: for who would not prefer four days of labour to six?
faults.why: The hiring benefit is turned into a rhetorical question and repeats the invented 'six'. It also adds a reason beyond the draft. 'Proper persons' and 'at all' add judgments the writer did not make.

faults.quote: instead of six
faults.why: The rewrite invents a fault of sense: it makes 'four days instead of six' a contrast that is wrong for a normal workplace. The notes report no mending.

faults.quote: such of our employers as are used to our present order of business
faults.why: The writer's 'clients' becomes 'employers', a different relation. Employers would not be the party to whom a team pitches a trial.

faults.quote: I am aware it might be thought hazardous
faults.why: Reasonable Austen cadence, but the piece overall leans on pastiche (Mr Collins, 'answer', 'give notice') without Austen's irony or balanced periods.

faults.quote: Our people are worn out with their work
faults.why: 'Worn out with their work' is fine, but the following clause 'as is often the way when men are over-worked' makes the sentence clumsy, and 'and is gone' reads awkwardly.

faults.quote: Fainter echo of the opening of Pride and Prejudice: a scheme for the people weighed by counting the cost aloud
faults.why: The echo claim is vague and does not match the opening of Pride and Prejudice. It is also filed under 'sense' though it is a move.

faults.quote: True echo of Mr Collins's proposal in Pride and Prejudice ch. 19
faults.why: Collins's proposal to Elizabeth has no relation to a workplace pitch with an objection answered. The 'true echo' is unsupported.

faults.quote: Free indirect discourse: “for who would not prefer four days of labour to six?” — cites Persuasion, ch. 20, ¶ 51
faults.why: A rhetorical question in first-person speech is not free indirect discourse, and the paragraph citation looks invented.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: A hesitation-word of the speaker's voice
faults.why: Fails to say which word, so it names no real change. 'The narrator's dry generalization' admits an added unrequested comment.

faults.quote: naming feeling by understatement, "worn out with their work,"
faults.why: The lesson claims understatement, but 'worn out' is already direct. The lesson also says the two closing sentences were joined, whereas the rewrite uses one sentence in that paragraph.

faults.quote: But we might make the trial for three months, and then judge of the wisdom of continuing it.
faults.why: The outline claims the objection is stated 'at its strongest' and that the risk is placed before the advantage, yet the rewrite keeps the original order. The outline and the rewrite disagree.

judge.verdict: The rewrite has a pleasant period-style surface, but it invents a six-day week, a long-held opinion, and an 'only objection of weight' claim, weakens the studies to hearsay, and swaps clients for employers. The notes misattribute sources and misclassify moves, so the teaching value is poor.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.

When Dana scratched our dinner, I was not at all sorry for it; on the contrary, I was relieved, and did not trouble myself to conceal it. I had been dreading it the whole week, and I am not proud of having done so.

I told her that it was of no consequence, and that we should do it another time; but I do not think that we shall, and was not sorry to be told so.

lessons: Your passage tells the whole story in five short, flat sentences, where Austen would have joined the same matter into balanced periods so that the relief carries its own weight. I let the narrator judge her own feeling in her abstract words ("of no consequence," "I am not proud of having done so") and closed with an ironic turn ("was not sorry to be told so") that says by understatement what your "I don't think we will" could only state. reading.kind: story (a very short one: a small event, a feeling, and a verdict)

outline.gist: Dana cancelled; the narrator was not upset but relieved.
The narrator had dreaded it all week and is not proud of it.
The narrator told Dana it was fine and they would do it another time.
The narrator does not think they will.

plan.gist: Dana cancelled; the narrator was not upset but relieved.
plan.why: Austen opens on the fact and lets the feeling follow at once, so the reader is put in possession of the situation before being asked to judge it; the small shock of relief lands harder when it is stated plainly and early.

plan.gist: The narrator had dreaded it all week and is not proud of it.
plan.why: She gives the reason for the relief immediately, so the reader is never left doubting the narrator's honesty; the admission of shame is the narrator's own character in miniature, and placing it here makes the politeness that follows read as a performance rather than a fact.

plan.gist: The narrator told Dana it was fine and they would do it another time.
plan.why: The reported words come after the private truth, so the reader hears them as a social formula and can measure them against what the narrator has just admitted — the lesson being that order of information creates irony without a word of comment.

plan.gist: The narrator does not think they will.
plan.why: The close reverses the polite promise in one flat sentence, leaving the reader with the gap between what was said and what is meant; Austen ends on the narrator's quiet judgment of the situation, not on sentiment, because the judgment is what the piece has been building toward.

faults.quote: and was not sorry to be told so
faults.why: Invents a new incident: Dana telling the narrator they will not reschedule. In the original the narrator alone doubts they will. This adds a fact and changes who holds the judgment.

faults.quote: and was not sorry to be told so
faults.why: The clause has no clear subject or sense. 'Told so' by whom? The sentence now contradicts the earlier 'I do not think that we shall', which was the narrator's own opinion. It also reads as a grammatical slip, since 'was' follows 'I do not think' with the subject dropped.

faults.quote: and did not trouble myself to conceal it
faults.why: Adds a new fact, that the narrator did not hide her relief. This conflicts with the polite 'of no consequence' she told Dana and with the shame she feels. It is not the voice commenting on what is there.

faults.quote: I was not at all sorry for it; on the contrary, I was relieved
faults.why: The writer says 'wasn't upset', not 'not sorry'. This is a small shift, and the 'on the contrary' stresses the relief more than the original does.

faults.quote: scratched our dinner
faults.why: 'Scratched' is a modern or colloquial verb for cancelling, and not Austen's idiom. It jars against the formal register around it.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: The writer says only that she was relieved and not upset; the voice, looking back, frames that relief in litotes
faults.why: Misdescribes the changes. It does not report the added 'did not trouble myself to conceal it' or the invented 'told so'. It calls litotes a liberty, which is not the real liberty.

faults.quote: Judgement in abstract nouns: “I told her that it was of no consequence” — cites Pride and Prejudice, ch. 10, ¶ 17
faults.why: The citation is dubious and not shown to match. 'Of no consequence' is a stock phrase, not an abstract-noun judgement. Paragraph 1 has no notes even though it carries the main changes.

faults.quote: closed with an ironic turn ("was not sorry to be told so")
faults.why: The lesson praises as a model the very clause that invents a fact and muddles the sense. It also claims the rewrite kept 'I am not proud of having done so', which is a clumsy phrase. The writer would learn a flawed move.

faults.quote: but I do not think that we shall, and was not sorry to be told so
faults.why: The close is meant to end on the flat verdict. The added clause blunts it and breaks the writer's ending, though the notes say the structure was kept.

faults.quote: I am not proud of having done so
faults.why: 'Done so' refers loosely to dreading, which is a feeling and not an act. It is awkward, and 'the whole week' is stiff.

judge.verdict: The rewrite is in a plausible Austenian register but invents an incident ('told so'), adds a claim about concealment, and leaves the final clause confused. The notes and lesson do not report these changes and praise the flawed ending.

Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
And at midnight Ryan sent unto me, saying, We must needs talk together. And I knew straightway what that meant: for the thing that he would say was known unto me.

And it came to pass on the morrow that we met at a place where they sell drink in the midst of the city. And he was there before me, looking upon his phone; and his countenance fell. And he said unto me, I am not ready for a thing that is grave and abiding; and it is not thou, but I: it is not in thee that the fault lieth.

And I would have wept, and yet I wept not; but I bowed my head, and said, It is well. Then I went home in the rain, and did eat a whole pint of ice cream.

And my friend that dwelleth with me said that I made too much of the matter. And peradventure I did. Yet the hurt thereof remained with me still.

And my friend that dwelleth with me said that I made too much of the matter. And peradventure I did. Yet the hurt thereof remained with me still.

lessons: The chief difference is that the King James Bible builds long sentences of balanced clauses joined by "and," where yours runs short and bare; so I have joined your first two sentences ("And at midnight Ryan sent unto me, saying, We must needs talk together") and given each turn a grave cadence. The voice gives feeling by its sign rather than naming it — "and his countenance fell" for "He looked nervous," "I would have wept, and yet I wept not" for "I wanted to cry but I didn't" — and that is what a reader feels most, because the sign shows the feeling where the name only tells it. Practise laying clause beside clause with "and," and letting the body carry the heart.

reading.kind: story (a short first-person account of a breakup)

outline.gist: A midnight text from Ryan: "we needed to talk"; the narrator knows at once what it means.
Next day, coffee shop downtown; Ryan already there on his phone, nervous; he says he isn't ready for something serious; "it's not you, it's me."
The narrator holds back tears, nods, says okay; walks home in the rain; eats a whole pint of ice cream.

outline.role: Verdict / close: the roommate's judgment and the narrator's answer
outline.gist: The roommate thinks it's an overreaction; maybe so, the narrator grants; but it still hurt.

plan.gist: The midnight text and the narrator's foreboding, stated plainly.
plan.why: The voice opens with the bare fact and lets the reader do the fearing with the narrator; a short sentence carrying dreadful news lands harder than any lament, and the reader is made a witness before being made a mourner.

plan.gist: The next day, the coffee shop, Ryan already there on his phone, nervous; his two sayings, "not ready for something serious" and "not you, it is me."
plan.why: The scene is given in order — time, place, his posture, his words — so the reader sees the small betrayals (already there, scrolling) beside the large one. The voice reports his speech as speech and adds no judgment of its own, letting the reader weigh the excuse; a narrator who argued would rob the reader of the verdict.

plan.gist: Tears withheld, a nod, "okay"; the walk home in the rain; the whole pint of ice cream.
plan.why: The restraint of "I wanted to cry but I didn't" earns the plainness of the pint; the voice knows that grief shown in small deeds convinces where named grief does not, and it keeps the writer's order so the hurt accumulates rather than being announced.

plan.role: Verdict / close: the roommate's judgment and the narrator's answer
plan.gist: The roommate calls it overreaction; the narrator concedes "maybe"; but it still hurt.
plan.why: The close sets the objection in another's mouth and answers it with the one thing that cannot be argued away — the fact of the hurt. The voice ends on that short clause because a concession followed by a plain assertion is how a case is closed: the reader has already granted it. The writer's order is kept throughout; nothing needs moving.

sense.problem: No fault of sense found: the persons are clear, the times agree (midnight text, next day, then the walk home), and no step the reader needs is missing — the reader knows from the opening line what the talk will be, and the passage confirms it.
sense.quote: Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.
sense.resolution: No mending needed. A possible echo: the narrator turned away and going home in the rain, then consoling themselves, faintly echoes the prodigal son's return and welcome (Luke 15) only in its homecoming and its small feast of ice cream — but there is no father running out, no welcome, and no repentance, so it is not a true echo; the rewrite should take nothing from it. The withholding of tears, the nodded "okay," and the hurt that outlasts the concession are the passage's own; the rewrite should keep them as they are, only spoken in the older tongue.

faults.quote: for the thing that he would say was known unto me.
faults.why: Adds a clause explaining the foreboding; the draft only says the narrator knew what 'we need to talk' meant. It restates the same thing and slightly changes it into foreknowledge of the content.

faults.quote: and his countenance fell.
faults.why: The draft says he 'looked nervous'. A fallen countenance means dejection or sadness, not nervousness, so the feeling is shifted. It also isn't a plain restatement.

faults.quote: I am not ready for a thing that is grave and abiding
faults.why: 'Something serious' becomes 'grave and abiding', which adds permanence the draft does not state.

faults.quote: it is not in thee that the fault lieth.
faults.why: Adds a redundant second statement of 'it wasn't me'. It's an expansion and not in the draft.

faults.quote: and said, It is well.
faults.why: 'Okay' is a nodding assent to the breakup; 'It is well' implies serene acceptance or approval, a different feeling. Also 'I just nodded' becomes 'bowed my head'.

faults.quote: And my friend that dwelleth with me
faults.why: 'Roommate' is rendered 'friend', adding a relationship the draft doesn't state. The tense 'dwelleth' is also present while the narration is past.

faults.quote: in the midst of the city
faults.why: 'Downtown' becomes 'in the midst of the city', which is fine; but 'a place where they sell drink' loses 'coffee' and is vague/comic.

faults.quote: And he was there before me, looking upon his phone
faults.why: Drops 'scrolling' sense lightly but acceptable; 'already there' kept. Minor. The larger issue is that 'Ryan sent unto me, saying' changes 'texted' to a message with no indication it was by phone, though acceptable.

faults.quote: And I would have wept, and yet I wept not
faults.why: A good KJV pattern, but the register overall is stagey pastiche, with no real scriptural rhythm. Lacks the parataxis and weight of real texts, and the draft's rain and ice cream are rendered flat.

faults.quote: did eat a whole pint of ice cream
faults.why: 'Pint of ice cream' is a jarring anachronism with no scriptural equivalent, and the 'did eat' is thin; the comedy is not controlled.

faults.quote: We must needs talk together.
faults.why: 'Must needs' is KJV-ish, but 'talk together' reads stilted; 'for the thing that he would say was known unto me' is awkward.

faults.quote: it is not thou, but I
faults.why: Grammatically ambiguous and stilted; 'it is not thou, but I' sounds wrong for the speaker of the line.

faults.quote: cites Leviticus 15:24
faults.why: Leviticus 15:24 concerns ritual uncleanness and has no parallel with 'it is not thou, but I'. The citation is false and inapt.

faults.quote: The narrator states plainly what the draft leaves to the reader's inference
faults.why: The notes claim a liberty that is not an actual change. The added clause is itself an addition, so the note misreports it and contradicts 'adding no fact'.

faults.quote: (no notes)
faults.why: Paragraphs 3 and 4 have no notes though they carry changes ('bowed my head', 'It is well', 'peradventure', 'friend'). 'Countenance fell' and 'grave and abiding' are also unnoted.

faults.quote: The voice gives feeling by its sign rather than naming it — "and his countenance fell" for "He looked nervous,"
faults.why: The lesson praises a change that actually alters the feeling (nervous to dejected), teaching a misleading lesson. It also gives little on structure.

faults.quote: it is not thou, but I: it is not in thee that the fault lieth.
faults.why: The notes claim no fault, but the rewrite adds 'fault' and 'grave and abiding', introducing a slight blame emphasis not in the draft.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the order of events but alters feelings (nervous becomes a fallen countenance, okay becomes 'It is well'), adds redundant clauses, and calls the roommate a 'friend'. The notes are thin, with a false Leviticus citation, and the lesson teaches a misleading example.

A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
Now there came a new family into the house that is beside us, at the end of the week that is past. And they have a great truck, and two little children with them. And their father seemeth a good man, but his sister is aloof.

And my mother baked for them cakes without delay. And she would know all that was of them: whence they came, and what they wrought for their bread, and whether they went up unto the house of the LORD.

And it came to pass that the father was a lawyer, and he was alone: he was put away from his wife. And my mother's countenance changed, and I knew just what she thought. For she hath sought to set me in marriage these many years.

rows.text: Now there came a new family into the house that is beside us, at the end of the week that is past. And they have a great truck, and two little children with them. And their father seemeth a good man, but his sister is aloof.

notes.text: Your first paragraph gives the new family a mother — 'the mom' beside 'the dad' — so the household has a married couple; your last paragraph says the dad is single, divorced. Both cannot stand. I made the 'mom' the dad's sister, the children's aunt, who moved in with the household to help with the two kids. This keeps her word, her wariness, the cookies and the matchmaking, and mends the contradiction: she is not his wife nor his former wife.
notes.after: And their father seemeth a good man, but his sister is aloof. … And the father is a lawyer, and he is alone: he is put away from his wife.

notes.text: The voice frames the wariness the writer named ('standoffish') as a settled manner in the person, a verdict in its own words; the writer's own word has no equivalent in the King James Bible.
notes.after: his sister is aloof

rows.text: And my mother baked for them cakes without delay. And she would know all that was of them: whence they came, and what they wrought for their bread, and whether they went up unto the house of the LORD.

notes.text: True echo of Ruth 1 — a newcomer is taken in and questioned, a household joined by a woman arriving among strangers. I took from it the plainness of the welcome and the naming of what the household is: who belongs to whom, and by what tie. The turn of a single man and a mother's matchmaking echoes no scriptural scene and is not forced into one.
notes.after: And she would know all that was of them: whence they came, and what they wrought for their bread, and whether they went up unto the house of the LORD.

notes.technique: Clauses laid side by side with “and”
notes.after: And my mother baked for them cakes without delay.
whether they went up unto the house of the LORD
whence they came, and what they wrought for their bread, and whether they went up unto the house of the LORD

rows.text: And it came to pass that the father was a lawyer, and he was alone: he was put away from his wife. And my mother's countenance changed, and I knew just what she thought. For she hath sought to set me in marriage these many years.

notes.text: The passage leaves unstated what the mother's 'look' means and why the dad's being a lawyer matters; the reader must supply the step from 'single' to 'setting me up'. No mending beyond the household: the final sentence supplies the answer, and the 'divorced' words supply the lawyer detail as the mother's measure of a prospect. I kept them in this order.
notes.after: And my mother's countenance changed, and I knew just what she thought.
And it came to pass that the father was a lawyer
he was alone: he was put away from his wife

notes.text: The voice keeps the narrator's certainty but states it in the Bible's own way ('just' for 'exactly'), and turns the report of the face into the sign of it, as the Bible gives feeling by its sign.
notes.after: And I knew just what she thought

lessons: The chief difference is joining: the King James Bible lays clause beside clause with "and" and tells the story in a grave cadence, where your draft reports each fact in a short, separate sentence. I opened nearly every sentence with "And", joined your short sentences into longer balanced clauses ("And their father seemeth a good man, but his sister is aloof"), and turned the turn of the story with "And it came to pass that the father was a lawyer." Practise saying one thing twice in parallel halves — "he was alone: he was put away from his wife" — and letting the sign of a feeling stand for the feeling itself, as in "my mother's countenance changed."

reading.kind: story (a short first-person anecdote or personal essay with a comic turn)

outline.gist: New family moves in next door; truck, two little kids; the dad seems nice; the mom is standoffish.
The narrator's mother bakes them cookies immediately, meaning to learn everything about them: origin, work, church.
Report: the dad is a lawyer and single — well, divorced; the mother gets a look; the narrator knows what she's thinking.
The mother has been trying to set the narrator up for years.

plan.gist: New family next door: truck, two little kids; the dad seems nice; the mom kind of standoffish.
plan.why: Scripture opens a story by placing the persons plainly before naming the turn; the reader must see the household before its fault can show, and the 'standoffish' note kept here prepares the surprise.

plan.gist: The mother bakes cookies at once and means to learn everything about them: whence they came, their work, their going to church.
plan.why: The voice would keep the writer's order and simply make the intent explicit, as the Bible tells a motive before it tells its fruit — so the cookies read as a search, not a gift, and the later look is understood.

plan.gist: The dad is a lawyer and single — well, divorced; the mother's look; the narrator knows her thought.
plan.why: This is the hinge; put it in its own short steep and let it strike. Here the family's 'mom' must be made someone other than the dad's wife — say the children's grandmother, or the dad's sister — so the single household and the standoffish woman both stand, and her distance turns to sense: a sister wary of a neighbour's inquiry.

plan.gist: She has been trying to set the narrator up for years.
plan.why: A close that ties the earlier fact to the new situation, as the parable ends by naming the lesson; kept last because in the writer's order it is the revelation of what the beginning was for.

sense.problem: Your first paragraph gives the new family a mother — 'the mom' beside 'the dad' — so the household has a married couple; your last paragraph says the dad is single, divorced. Both cannot stand.
sense.quote: The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish. … It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single.
sense.resolution: Make the 'mom' the children's grandmother, or the dad's sister who lives with him, and say so in a word — she moved in with her brother's household to help with the two kids, say. Least change: it keeps her word and her wariness, keeps the cookies and the matchmaking, and mends the contradiction. She must not be called his wife nor his former wife, for the single divorced dad rules those out.

sense.problem: The passage leaves unstated what the mother's 'look' means and why the dad's being a lawyer matters; the reader must supply the step from 'single' to 'setting me up'.
sense.quote: My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking.
sense.resolution: No fault of sense beyond the one above: the final sentence supplies the answer, and the 'divorced' words supply the lawyer detail as the mother's measure of a prospect. Keep them in this order; only the household must be mended.

sense.problem: Echo of a scene of the author's.
sense.quote: She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.
sense.resolution: True echo of Ruth 1 — a newcomer is taken in and questioned, and 'whither thou goest' is a household joined by a woman arriving among strangers; the rewrite may take from it the plainness of the welcome and the naming of what the household is: who belongs to whom, and by what tie. The turn itself — a single man, a mother's matchmaking — echoes no scriptural scene and should not be forced into one.

faults.quote: his sister is aloof
faults.why: The mending invents a sister. The writer's 'mom' is made an aunt who lives with the household, a new fact. The mending is reported, but it is an invention that could have been avoided or marked more lightly. The children's 'mom' is also lost.

faults.quote: and he was alone: he was put away from his wife
faults.why: 'Well, divorced' is the writer's self-correction, a comic beat. 'Put away from his wife' loses the hesitation and suggests the wife was cast off, shifting blame onto the dad. It also adds a moral judgment.

faults.quote: cakes
faults.why: The writer's 'cookies' becomes 'cakes', a shift in the object. It is acceptable for the era, but not noted as a liberty.

faults.quote: at the end of the week that is past
faults.why: 'Last weekend' becomes the end of the week; this is slightly imprecise. 'Now there came' also adds an opening not in the original.

faults.quote: And my mother's countenance changed, and I knew just what she thought.
faults.why: The writer's 'look' is not necessarily a change of countenance. Also dropped is the 'got this look' sense of knowing exactly; 'just' is weak for 'exactly'. The 'kind of' softening of 'standoffish' is lost with 'aloof'.

faults.quote: And their father seemeth a good man
faults.why: 'Seemeth' is a thin archaism, and 'seemeth a good man' is not KJV usage. The 'nice' sense is flattened to 'good' (moral rather than pleasant). 'Hath sought to set me in marriage these many years' is serviceable but pastiche; 'wrought for their bread' is apt.

faults.quote: And it came to pass that the father was a lawyer
faults.why: 'It came to pass' is used for an event, not a discovery of fact; the KJV uses it for occurrences, so it is misapplied. 'Lawyer' is also used in the KJV, but in a different sense (expert in the law).

faults.quote: he was put away from his wife
faults.why: In the KJV, 'put away' refers to the husband divorcing the wife (Matt 5:32). Here it reads as though the husband was put away by her, which is a role inversion and a malapropism.

faults.quote: whether they went up unto the house of the LORD
faults.why: 'Went up' is a slightly forced pilgrimage idiom for ordinary church-going, which is a mild comic mismatch. It is arguably acceptable.

faults.quote: No mending beyond the household: the final sentence supplies the answer, and the 'divorced' words supply the lawyer detail as the mother's measure of a prospect.
faults.why: Muddled note. The mending of the contradiction itself is reasonable, but this note reads as garbled and invents a rationale about the lawyer detail.

faults.quote: True echo of Ruth 1 — a newcomer is taken in and questioned
faults.why: Ruth 1 is not about a neighbor's welcome with questions; it is a stretched, mislabelled source, and this note is a 'sense' note rather than a move. The Ezekiel 3:11, John 7:27, 2 Kings 15:12 and 1 Samuel 4:21 citations for single phrases are loose: they do not model the cited constructions.

faults.quote: The voice frames the wariness the writer named ('standoffish') as a settled manner in the person, a verdict in its own words; the writer's own word has no equivalent in the King James Bible.
faults.why: The liberty note is vague and does not match the actual change (the mom became a sister and 'standoffish' became 'aloof'). The final-paragraph liberty note misdescribes 'just' for 'exactly' as a voice move.

faults.quote: I opened nearly every sentence with "And"
faults.why: The lesson is sound on and-joining, but the claim that the short sentences were joined into longer clauses is only partly true, since the rewrite stays choppy. 'The sign of a feeling' is the only other lesson, so the takeaway is limited. The outline's grandmother/sister option goes unexplained when the rewrite chose the sister.

faults.quote: And the father was a lawyer, and he was alone
faults.why: The writer's comic turn ('Well, divorced.') and the final punch ('trying to set me up') are blunted by the solemn cadence, and the outline's talk of making it 'its own short steep' is not done.

judge.verdict: A competent KJV pastiche that keeps the order and mends the contradiction by inventing a sister, but the 'put away' inversion, the lost comic hesitation, loose scriptural citations and muddled notes weaken it. The teaching is limited to and-joining and parallelism.

Hi team,

Quick update: the launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday. Legal still hasn't signed off on the pricing page, and I don't want us shipping without it.

Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon. If you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.

Thanks,
Sam
rewrite:
Unto the company, greeting.

Behold, the day of the launch is changed, and it is moved from Tuesday unto Thursday. For the counsel in the law hath not yet set his seal upon the page of the prices, and I would not that we send it forth without him.

Have thy parts of the work finished by the sixth day at noon, and let no man be slack therein. And if any man be hindered, let him tell me this day, and not tarry until the morrow.

I give you thanks. The salutation of me Sam with mine own hand.

rows.text: Unto the company, greeting.

Behold, the day of the launch is changed, and it is moved from Tuesday unto Thursday. For the counsel in the law hath not yet set his seal upon the page of the prices, and I would not that we send it forth without him.

notes.after: Behold, the day of the launch is changed, and it is moved from Tuesday unto Thursday.
it is moved from Tuesday unto Thursday

notes.text: The voice opens the news with an attention-call the writer's plain statement invites: the framing marks the announcement as a turning of the matter, in the way the Bible marks a change of days.
notes.after: Behold, the day of the launch is changed, and it is moved from Tuesday unto Thursday.

rows.text: Have thy parts of the work finished by the sixth day at noon, and let no man be slack therein. And if any man be hindered, let him tell me this day, and not tarry until the morrow.

notes.after: Have thy parts of the work finished by the sixth day at noon, and let no man be slack therein.

rows.text: I give you thanks. The salutation of me Sam with mine own hand.

lessons: Your passage is a quick work memo; the King James Bible's manner is slow and grave, so each short directive becomes a full clause ("Have thy parts of the work finished by the sixth day at noon, and let no man be slack therein"). Add "and" to lay clause beside clause, and open the news with "behold," which the voice uses to mark a turn of the matter; the closing follows the epistle form with a salutation in the writer's own hand. Practise turning one short sentence into two balanced halves joined by "and"—as in "let him tell me this day, and not tarry until the morrow"—so each matter lands twice, first in one set of words, then in other words.

reading.kind: email — a short work update from a lead to their team

outline.gist: "Hi team" — addresses the recipients collectively
The launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday
Legal has not signed off on the pricing page, and Sam won't ship without that sign-off
Have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday noon
If blocked, say so today, not tomorrow
"Thanks, Sam"

plan.gist: "Hi team" — addresses the recipients collectively
plan.why: The King James Bible opens a letter by naming those addressed, so each reader knows at once that the word is for them; it keeps the writer's order and his brevity, adding no title or flourish the matter does not carry.

plan.gist: The launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday
plan.why: The one thing that changes for the reader is put first, as the epistles state the matter in hand before they argue it: a reader who learns only one line should learn the change. The writer already leads with it; the plan keeps that and only sharpens the contrast of the two days.

plan.gist: Legal has not signed off on the pricing page, and Sam won't ship without that sign-off
plan.why: A new date without a cause breeds rumour and repeated questions; the cause follows the news immediately, as the King James Bible gives the ground before the charge ("for this cause"), so the reader sees the move is necessity and not caprice. It is placed after the news, not before, because the reader cares what changed before why.

plan.gist: Have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday noon
plan.why: Only now, the reason being known, does the ask land as reasonable rather than arbitrary; the Bible binds an instruction to the ground already laid ("therefore"), which is how an ask is obeyed rather than resented. The writer's order is kept: news, reason, then duty.

plan.gist: If blocked, say so today, not tomorrow
plan.why: A command with a time in it needs a way out for the one who cannot keep it, or it produces silence and late failure; the King James Bible habitually sets the condition plainly ("if thou be...") and names the day, so the reader cannot plead the term was vague. It closes the ask as the law closes a statute — with the exception and its hour.

plan.gist: "Thanks, Sam"
plan.why: A letter ends with a greeting and the sender's name, as the Pauline epistles do, so the reader knows whose word binds them and that goodwill attends it. The writer's own close is kept, needing nothing but to stand as a farewell in its own short line.

faults.quote: by the sixth day at noon
faults.why: Wednesday is rendered as 'the sixth day'. In a week where Tuesday and Thursday are named, Wednesday is the fourth day (or third, counting from Monday), not the sixth. This changes the deadline to something wrong (Friday) and contradicts the Thursday launch.

faults.quote: For the counsel in the law hath not yet set his seal upon the page of the prices
faults.why: 'Legal' (a team or department) becomes a single male 'counsel', and the pricing page becomes 'the page of the prices'. This is an acceptable archaism but loses the department sense and is somewhat unclear.

faults.quote: and let no man be slack therein
faults.why: Adds an exhortation not in the writer's note (nobody is told to avoid slackness). It adds a stern tone the writer did not have.

faults.quote: I give you thanks.
faults.why: The writer's 'Thanks' is a light close; the rendering is acceptable but the following line adds more than the draft offers.

faults.quote: The salutation of me Sam with mine own hand.
faults.why: Borrowed from Paul (1 Cor 16:21), it is an addition: the 'own hand' claim is invented, and 'of me Sam' is garbled ('The salutation of me Paul' is the original form, but the grammar here reads awkwardly).

faults.quote: Unto the company, greeting.
faults.why: 'Company' replaces 'team' and the greeting becomes a formula. Acceptable, but 'company' implies the whole firm rather than the team.

faults.quote: Have thy parts of the work finished
faults.why: 'Thy' is singular and addresses a plural team; the previous line says 'the company' and the later 'you' and 'him'. Mixed number is inconsistent and the KJV uses 'your' for plurals. 'Have your parts' would be correct.

faults.quote: from Tuesday unto Thursday
faults.why: Modern day names in a KJV register are an anachronism that jars; the KJV would say 'the third day'. The rewrite uses 'sixth day' for Wednesday but modern names for Tuesday and Thursday, which is inconsistent.

faults.quote: I would not that we send it forth without him
faults.why: 'Him' refers to the counsel but the thing sent is the page or the launch; 'it' is unclear. It also reads as a slightly clumsy KJV imitation.

faults.quote: Behold, the day of the launch is changed, and it is moved
faults.why: 'Is changed' and 'is moved' repeat the same meaning with a redundant pairing, padding the news.

faults.quote: cites Jeremiah 4:24
faults.why: The verse is cited as a source for 'Behold' with a sentence the Bible does not contain; the note labels are generic ('Behold, lo, verily') and the quoted passage is the rewrite's own line. Jeremiah 4:24 is about mountains trembling and is only loosely apt.

faults.quote: cites Mark 1:41
faults.why: Mark 1:41 (Jesus healing the leper) is not an apt source for 'unto' or for moving a date, and the note's heading does not match the quoted line.

faults.quote: cites Leviticus 23:3
faults.why: This verse is about the sabbath, not 'thou and thee, -eth and -est', and the quoted sentence uses neither -eth nor -est; the note does not match the content.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 1:
  (no notes)
faults.why: No notes for the opening and closing paragraphs, though the rewrite adds the salutation 'with mine own hand' and 'Unto the company', which are changes that should be reported.

faults.quote: Add "and" to lay clause beside clause
faults.why: This is generic and not a transferable lesson. The lesson says 'balanced halves' but the closing line it cites is not clearly distinct from the draft's own 'today, not tomorrow'. The how_it_is_built section claims the rewrite kept the writer's order, but the rewrite adds a sentence the plan does not describe.

faults.quote: and let no man be slack therein. And if any man be hindered
faults.why: The order is kept, but the added exhortation shifts the request toward a command with a threat and loosens the two-part request.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the email's order and has some KJV flavour, but it turns Wednesday into 'the sixth day' (a factual error), mixes thy/you and modern day names, and adds invented content ('own hand', 'let no man be slack'). The notes cite verses that do not support the moves named and the lesson is thin.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

rewrite:
I counsel that our town should shut Main Street to waggons upon the weekends of the summer. For to set a waggon in the midst of the town is a sore travail and a dream: and the ways that run beside it are too narrow for the carriages of the children.

And other towns have shut their streets upon the weekends, and their booths have done better since they shut them. Some of the merchants will say, Our guests cannot come unto us: but they will be used to it. For the more part of men walk from the garage upon the weekends, and are not letted: and the booths of the other towns have done better since they shut their streets.

reading.kind: argument (a short op-ed style proposal to a town)

outline.gist: Close Main Street to cars on weekends.
