plan.gist: That Main Street be closed to cars on summer weekends.
plan.why: The KJV puts the matter at issue first, in one plain sentence, so the reader knows from the start what is being asked and can weigh everything after it against that. This is the writer's own order and it is kept; the only change is that the claim now names the time as the trial does.

plan.gist: Parking downtown is hard to come by.
plan.why: A claim is followed by its causes, for a reader will not judge a remedy until he grants the ill. The KJV names the trouble plainly and lets the pain stand before the cure; the writer already does this and keeps it.

plan.gist: The sidewalks are too narrow for strollers.
plan.why: The second reason should stand beside the first, not be buried, so the reader sees that the trouble is not one complaint but two — room for the car and room for the walker. The KJV pairs like with like before drawing a conclusion from the pair.

plan.gist: Other towns have closed their main streets on weekends, and their shops have done better since.
plan.why: The KJV gives proof before it suffers an objection, so that the reader has something to hold when the counter-case comes. Here the evidence is also made to match the proposal (weekends), which teaches that a proof must be of the very thing claimed, or the reader will notice the gap.

plan.gist: The business owners will say customers cannot come to them.
plan.why: The KJV names the strongest adversary fairly, in his own words, before answering him; an objection stated in someone else's mouth and then dismissed looks like evasion, and the reader who is that someone stops listening. Putting it in its place — after the proof, before the answer — is the writer's order, kept.

plan.gist: Weekend customers come on foot from the garage, which stays open; and in the other towns the shops did better for it.
plan.why: An answer must do more than promise patience: it must take away the harm alleged. The KJV answers with the two facts already given — the garage and the other towns — so the reader sees the objection weighed and found lighter than the gain. This replaces the bare "they'll get used to it."

plan.gist: Let us try it this summer.
plan.why: The close makes the claim an act, and asks only for a trial — the smallest thing that settles the question the town is arguing. The KJV ends on the deed to be done, so the reader is left with something he can do and with the argument already answered behind him. Kept from the writer, save that the summer is now named consistently as a trial of weekends.

sense.problem: Your first sentence proposes closing Main Street "on weekends," and your last proposes to try it "this summer." But the objections you answer are about all customers, all the time: "customers can't get to them," and "most people walk from the garage anyway." A reader cannot tell whether you mean weekends only, or the whole summer, weekends and weekdays alike. The reply about the garage actually undercuts the weekend proposal: if most people walk from the garage already, the parking problem the proposal is meant to solve seems smaller than you said, and a shopkeeper will turn your own sentence against you.
sense.quote: Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends. ... We should try it this summer. ... most people walk from the garage anyway.
sense.resolution: Make the trial match the proposal: "close Main Street to cars on summer weekends," or, if you mean weekends, say the trial runs through the summer's weekends. Then tie the garage sentence to the weekend case it actually supports — that weekend customers who park in the garage and walk in are unharmed — so it answers the objection instead of giving the objector his answer.

sense.problem: Your evidence that closing works — "Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever" — is laid against the objection without ever being aimed at it. The reader is not told what "this" is: weekends only, or permanently? Nor is he told how we are to know the shops' improvement is due to the closed street rather than to anything else. Since the whole claim rests on those other towns, the reader needs one step more than you give him.
sense.quote: Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.
sense.resolution: Say plainly what the other towns did — closed their main streets on weekends, as you propose — so that the example is the same measure as the proposal; and make the inference modest: their shops "have done better since," which is what a comparison to the town's own past before the closing can support. That is the least change that makes the evidence bear on the claim.

sense.problem: The strongest objection is answered by dismissal — "But they'll get used to it" — which concedes that the harm is real and only says it will pass. A reader who owns a shop, or who shops, is given no reason to think the harm is small or outweighed, and the objection is never really put (it is assumed, in the voice of others), so it cannot be answered.
sense.quote: Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it.
sense.resolution: Keep the objection, but answer it with what the passage already has: weekend customers can still reach the shops on foot from the garage, and the other towns' shops did better after closing. That removes the fault — an answered objection — without adding a fact you did not already give.

This keeps the writer's order and adds no new evidence.

sense.problem: “Parking downtown is a nightmare” and “most people walk from the garage anyway” sit awkwardly together: if most people park in the garage and walk, the nightmare and the walk are the same fact described two ways, and the passage does not say so.
sense.quote: Parking downtown is a nightmare ... most people walk from the garage anyway.
sense.resolution: The same mending as above resolves it: name the garage in the first paragraph (“parking downtown is a nightmare — the garage fills and the spillover is worse”), so that the later sentence about walking from the garage follows from the stated problem rather than contradicting it. A reader who has been told the garage is where the parking is will read the walk from it as the solution, not the objection.

sense.problem: No true echo of a scene of Obama's is present in the passage as written; the closest is the structure of anticipating an objection and answering it fairly, which belongs to the eulogies and the Tucson memorial, but the passage does not reach it because the objection is dismissed rather than answered.
sense.quote: Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it.

What the rewrite may take from it is the fairness of stating the objection as the objectors would state it, affirming that the worry is legitimate before answering it with the same facts already on the table — not a new argument, just the right placement. faults.quote: We have nothing to lose by trying it, and it costs us nothing to try.

reading.kind: argument (a short proposal with an objection and a proposed test)

outline.gist: We should switch to a four-day week.
People are burned out; the best engineer just quit.
Studies show productivity stays the same or rises.
It would help with hiring.
It's risky, and clients might not like it.
Try it for three months and see.

plan.gist: We should switch to a four-day week — stated up front, unchanged.
plan.why: Obama names the proposition first so every reason after it lands as support for something the reader already holds in mind; a reader who has to assemble the claim from the reasons spends attention on sorting rather than weighing.

plan.gist: The cost we already pay: people are burned out, and our best engineer just quit.
plan.why: He starts from what the audience can see and feel — the concrete loss — before any study, because a shared cost makes the audience a 'we' with a stake, and the argument then asks them to protect something rather than to adopt a theory. The engineer's departure is kept as the vivid, specific instance that carries the general claim of burnout.

plan.gist: Studies show productivity holds or rises.
plan.why: Only after the cost is felt does he bring the external proof, and he brings something for the doubter in the room as well as the believer — the boss or client who fears the cost of the change. Evidence placed after the shared concern answers a fear the reader already has rather than one he has to be talked into.

plan.gist: It would help with hiring.
plan.why: This widens the audience: the first reason speaks to those already worn down, this one to whoever must fill the empty seat. Obama routinely stacks reasons that reach different listeners, so no one in the room is left with only a general appeal to agree with.

plan.gist: It's risky and clients might not like it — so try it for three months and see.
plan.why: He states the strongest objection in its strongest form and answers it with a test rather than a denial, because conceding the risk costs little and buys credibility for everything else; a proposal scaled to three months lets a cautious listener say yes to the experiment without saying yes to the change. The answer also returns the decision to the audience as something they can act on, which is where Obama's arguments are built to end.

plan.gist: Adopt the trial — decide to try it.
plan.why: The close is the small, doable ask that follows from the concession, so the audience leaves with a motion rather than an opinion. Keeping the writer's sequence throughout preserves the logic of cost, proof, wider benefit, doubt, answer; only the framing sharpens the sense that the last line is a request for a decision, not a hedge.

faults.quote: Here's the thing: I think we should move to a week of four working days.
faults.why: "Here's the thing" is a generic casual opener, not distinctively Obama. His typical openers are "Now," "Let me be clear," or "Look," and the hedge "I think" is not his stance. "A week of four working days" is stilted, not his plain idiom.

faults.quote: The studies show productivity holds steady or rises; and it would help us bring on the people we need.
faults.why: The rewrite is nearly the writer's text, lightly reworded. It lacks Obama's cadence: triads, parallelism, "that's what" turns, and the balanced "on the one hand / on the other" concession. It reads as modern prose with a casual tag.

faults.quote: productivity holds steady or rises; and it would help
faults.why: A semicolon followed by "and" is a punctuation misstep, awkward rather than idiomatic.

faults.quote: our best engineer just walked out the door
faults.why: "Walked out the door" implies leaving abruptly or angrily; the writer said only "quit." Mild shift in tone.

faults.quote: and see how it goes
faults.why: Adds a small softening phrase. The shift is minor, but it makes the closing less decisive.

faults.quote: cites Weekly Address, 28 July 2012, ¶ 4
faults.why: This citation is not credible for "Here's the thing"; it is a precise-looking source that does not clearly support the move. Only one move is noted for the whole rewrite, and it is weak.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: The voice's plain talk to the listener
faults.why: The notes name no change to the concession or the closing, and they do not mention that the paragraphs were merged to remove a break, nor the vague "how it goes." They are thin compared with what was changed.

faults.quote: Here's the thing: I think we should move to a week of four working days. Our people are burned out,
faults.why: The how_it_is_built claims the voice would put the shared cost first and build a call. The rewrite does none of that. It keeps the writer's order and adds no turn, so the outline describes a rewrite that was not done.

faults.quote: Practice opening with a turn toward the listener and closing each paragraph on the action, not just the fact.
faults.why: The lesson praises "the second paragraph" answering risk, but the rewrite merged everything into one paragraph. It also cites "Our people are burned out" as naming the cost before the verdict, though the verdict comes first. The lesson contradicts the text.

judge.verdict: A faithful but near-verbatim light edit with a generic "Here's the thing" opener; it barely sounds like Obama. The notes, outline and lesson describe moves that are not in the rewrite and contradict it, so the teaching value is weak.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.
rewrite:
When Dana called off our dinner, I wasn't upset in the least. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been holding my breath about it all week, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine and we'd make a time for it down the road. But I don't think we will.

rows.text: When Dana called off our dinner, I wasn't upset in the least. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been holding my breath about it all week, and I'm not proud of that.
I told her it was fine and we'd make a time for it down the road. But I don't think we will.

lessons: The writer's draft is bare and skips over the feeling it confesses. Obama's manner names the feeling plainly first ("Honestly, I was relieved"), then turns to the confession with an antithesis ("not this, but that" in "holding my breath... and I'm not proud of that"), and finally lands the second paragraph on a quiet verdict ("But I don't think we will") that lets the reservation stand without overstating it. Practise the turn: tell the small truth plainly, then let the harder truth follow as its opposite.

reading.kind: other — a short personal account in the first person: four sentences of news and inward feeling, closer to a letter or a diary entry than to a story or an argument.

outline.gist: Dana cancelled the dinner.
The writer was not upset; he was relieved.
He had dreaded it all week and is not proud of it.
That it was fine, and they would do it another time.
He doubts they will.

plan.role: Setting the scene plainly, and the turn
plan.gist: Dana cancelled; the writer was not upset.
plan.why: Start with the small fact everyone can see, then the reaction that surprises — the reader leans in to learn why the reaction is odd, and nothing has been claimed yet that must be defended.

plan.role: The honest admission, owned before it can be used against him
plan.gist: He was relieved; he had dreaded it all week; he is not proud of it.
plan.why: Name the least flattering fact yourself and grant its weight, so the reader trusts the rest; a confession offered up front cannot be sprung on you later. The admission also supplies the reason for the relief, answering the question the first part raised.

plan.role: What was said, set against what was felt
plan.gist: He told her it was fine and they would do it another time.
plan.why: Place the polite words right after the confession so the reader sees the gap between the two without being told what to make of it; the contrast does the work, and the writer keeps his claim modest — he reports the words, not a judgment of them.

plan.role: The quiet close, hedged and unresolved
plan.gist: He does not think they will do it another time.
plan.why: End on the smallest, most honest sentence — a doubt, not a verdict — so the piece lands with the weight of something still open; the hedge keeps it true to what he actually knows.

faults.quote: When Dana called off our dinner, I wasn't upset in the least. Honestly, I was relieved.
faults.why: This is almost the writer's own text with a few synonyms swapped. There is no Obama cadence: no balanced clauses, no 'Now,' or 'Look,' pivot, no reflective widening of the point. It reads as modern prose in a thin costume.

faults.quote: I'd been holding my breath about it all week
faults.why: This replaces 'dreading' with a mild idiom. It weakens the specific feeling and adds no Obama move. 'Holding my breath' usually suggests anticipation or hope, so it blurs the dread.

faults.quote: holding my breath about it all week
faults.why: 'Dreading' is changed to a phrase that can mean nervous hope, so the feeling is not carried to the same degree or direction.

faults.quote: we'd make a time for it down the road
faults.why: 'Make a time' is slightly off idiom; 'find a time' or 'set a date' is usual. 'Down the road' also changes 'another time' into something vaguer and more folksy.

faults.quote: But I don't think we will.
faults.why: Adding 'But' is a small gesture toward Obama's rhythm, but the close is otherwise unchanged. The writer's own 'I don't think we will' is not given Obama's reflective, self-implicating turn.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 1:

Paragraph 2:

faults.why: The rewrite changes several phrases and adds 'But', yet the notes name no moves or sources. The writer cannot see what changed or why.

faults.quote: Obama's manner names the feeling plainly first ("Honestly, I was relieved"), then turns to the confession with an antithesis ("not this, but that" in "holding my breath... and I'm not proud of that")
faults.why: The lesson credits Obama with moves that were in the writer's draft ('Honestly, I was relieved'). The claimed antithesis is not in the rewrite. The lesson also says the draft 'skips over the feeling', which is false. The outline's advice is sound, but the rewrite does not carry it out.

faults.quote: I told her it was fine and we'd make a time for it down the road.
faults.why: The outline calls for setting the polite words against the feeling, and the rewrite does not sharpen or frame that contrast. It is kept as in the draft, which is acceptable but adds nothing.

The next day we met at a coffee-house downtown, and he was there before me, working over his telephone and looking as if he'd been sentenced, and I saw in a minute how the land lay. He said he wasn't ready for anything serious, and he said it wasn't me, it was him, which is a way he has.

notes.after: he said it wasn't me, it was him, which is a way he has.

notes.text: The voice frames Ryan's move as a settled habit of his, a verdict on what the writer gave (the easy excuse) rather than a new fact; it lands the joke deadpan at the end of the clause.
notes.after: which is a way he has

rows.text: I wanted to cry, but I didn't; I just nodded and said all right, and then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice-cream.

rows.text: My roommate said I was making too much of it, and maybe I was, but it hurt all the same.

lessons: The chief difference is that your sentences are short and unjoined, each one a bare fact, where Twain piles clauses on "," and "and" until the turn comes at the end of a long run. reading.kind: story (a first-person short narrative — a breakup told in brief scenes)

outline.gist: A midnight text: "we need to talk," and the narrator knows at once what it means.
Next day, a coffee shop downtown; Ryan is already there, scrolling, nervous.
Ryan says he isn't ready for something serious; "it isn't you, it's me."
The narrator wants to cry but doesn't; nods, says okay.
She walks home in the rain and eats a whole pint of ice cream.
The roommate says she's overreacting; she grants it maybe, but it still hurt.

plan.gist: The midnight text and her instant certainty of what it means.
plan.why: Twain opens with a plain fact the reader can feel in the gut and lets the reader do the arithmetic of doom — a claim stated flatly and early hooks harder than a slow approach, because the reader wants to see it proved.

plan.gist: The coffee shop, Ryan already there, scrolling, nervous.
plan.why: Treacherous news needs a small, ordinary stage; giving just enough setting (where, who, what he's doing) lets the reader see the scene, and the small detail of the scrolling phone does the work of a page of description — evidence, placed before the claim, so the reader believes it.

plan.gist: Ryan's speech: not ready for something serious; it isn't you, it's me.
plan.why: Twain would keep the other man's own words and let them condemn themselves; quoting the cliché verbatim is stronger evidence than any summary of it, because the reader hears exactly what she heard.

plan.gist: She wants to cry, doesn't; nods, says okay.
plan.why: Understatement beats declaration: showing the held-back feeling and the two flat words lets the reader supply the grief, which is the Twain way of making a reader feel a thing without ever naming it.

plan.gist: Walking home in the rain; a whole pint of ice cream.
plan.why: Keep this order: after the restraint comes the release, and the concrete comic detail (the whole pint) lets the body say what the mouth wouldn't — a joke that also lands as grief, which is exactly how Twain gets sadness past the reader's guard.

plan.gist: The roommate says she's overreacting; maybe she is, but it still hurt.
plan.why: Twain would raise the objection himself before the reader does, grant it honestly, and then quietly answer it with the last three words — letting the objection stand and the hurt stand beside it; the close is short and flat, because a plain final sentence carries more weight than a declaration.

sense.problem: No fault of sense is present: persons, times and sequence all agree, and nothing needed is withheld.
sense.quote: My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
sense.resolution: No mending needed. (Note only, not a sense fault: the passage never says where Ryan and the narrator stood — boyfriend, or merely 'seeing' — before the breakup. That is deliberate and the story works without it; if the writer wants it pinned, one word in the first paragraph — 'my boyfriend' or 'the guy I'd been seeing' — would do it, and nothing else would change.)

sense.problem: Echo, not fault: a couple ending at a public place, the other party's easy excuse, and the plain-spoken hurt afterward look for a Twain scene to lean on.
sense.quote: He said it wasn't me, it was him.
sense.resolution: The nearest is the raft friendship Huck and Jim share and the world's judgment on it — Twain's habit of putting a stubborn, decent feeling against what everyone says is proper. The rewrite may take from it the method, not the matter: keep the narrator's feeling plain and unapologetic while the roommate plays the voice of 'what everybody thinks,' and let the narrator grant the objection mildly without surrendering the hurt. Tom whitewashing the fence is only a faint parallel (Ryan's chore of ending things, dumped on her to absorb), so take little from it beyond the lesson that a flat, deadpan account of an unfair transaction is funnier and truer than complaint.

faults.quote: which is a way he has
faults.why: This makes the 'it's not you, it's me' line a habit of Ryan's. The writer never said so, so it adds a fact about his character. The notes call it a 'liberty' but defend it as commentary.

faults.quote: I judge a body don't send word at that hour for any pleasant purpose, and he didn't.
faults.why: This adds a sentence of narratorial reasoning. The note on this paragraph never reports it. 'Past midnight' also shifts the writer's 'at midnight'.

faults.quote: I saw in a minute how the land lay
faults.why: The narrator already 'knew right away' what the text meant, so this repeats the same realisation. It also shifts the timing of when she understood.

faults.quote: My roommate said I was making too much of it
faults.why: The original says the roommate 'thought' she was overreacting. Changing it to 'said' alters what is told, though only slightly.

faults.quote: I judge a body don't send word at that hour
faults.why: This is Huck Finn's backwoods dialect dropped into an otherwise standard narrator ('I wanted to cry, but I didn't'). The register is inconsistent, and it reads as a costume phrase rather than Twain's controlled narration.

faults.quote: I just nodded and said all right, and then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice-cream.
faults.why: Almost unchanged from the original apart from the added commas and 'and then'. The last paragraphs have little Twain texture: no extended simile, no deadpan exaggeration, no hyperbole.

faults.quote: working over his telephone
faults.why: 'Working over' is an odd fit for scrolling. It is vague and slightly comic, and it blurs the original's casual 'scrolling on his phone'.

faults.quote: looking as if he'd been sentenced
faults.why: This is a heavier image than 'nervous'. It tilts the tone toward mockery of Ryan and slightly undercuts the narrator's hurt.

faults.quote: cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 8, ¶ 4
faults.why: This citation is implausible for 'which is a way he has'. It looks invented rather than matched to a real passage.

faults.quote: cites The Innocents Abroad, ch. 38, ¶ 2
faults.why: No real cumulative sentence in this passage is shown to match the cited place. The citation is unverifiable and probably decorative.

faults.quote: Echo, not fault: a couple ending at a public place, the other party's easy excuse, and the plain-spoken hurt afterward call for a Twain scene to lean on. The nearest is the raft friendship in Huckleberry Finn
faults.why: The note is muddled. A raft friendship and Tom whitewashing the fence are not apt parallels for a breakup, and the 'sense' label does not fit what the note says.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 4:
  (no notes)
faults.why: Nothing is said about the concession-then-hurt sentence, the closing move the lesson stresses. The 'sentenced' image, the added aside in paragraph 1, and other changes are also unreported.

faults.quote: the deadline joke sits flat at the end
faults.why: There is no 'deadline' joke. The image is 'sentenced', and it sits mid-sentence, not at the end. The lesson also says the nervousness is 'shown, not named', yet the image is itself a gloss on it. The lesson is partly inaccurate.

faults.quote: Twain would keep the other man's own words and let them condemn themselves
faults.why: The outline recommends quoting Ryan verbatim, but the rewrite keeps indirect speech and adds 'a way he has' instead. The rewrite does not follow its own guidance.

judge.verdict: A readable, faithful-enough Twain pastiche with a good closing run-together sentence. But it adds an invented trait for Ryan and an unreported aside, mixes dialect with standard narration, and has dubious citations and a muddled note. The lesson is partly inaccurate.

rows.text: A new family moved in next door last Saturday, with a monstrous great truck and two little children. The man seemed pleasant enough, and his sister, which helps with the two little ones, seemed kind of offish.

notes.text: Your first paragraph gives the new family a 'dad' and a 'mom'; your third says the dad is single — divorced. A household with a mother in it cannot also have a divorced father alone at its head, and the mother's matchmaking turns on his being free. I made the standoffish woman the dad's sister (she moved in to help with the two little kids), not the children's mother; that removes the contradiction, leaves the dad single and divorced as the close needs, and fits a divorced father with a household big enough for another adult.
notes.after: The man seemed pleasant enough, and his sister, which helps with the two little ones, seemed kind of offish.

rows.text: My mother baked them cakes right off, all in one whoosh, as the mother does — she wanted to find out everything about them: where they come from, what they done for work, whether they went to church.

notes.text: The deadpan generalization about the mother's way of doing things, stated flatly; it frames the cookie call she is about to make, adding no new fact.
notes.after: all in one whoosh, as the mother does

rows.text: She came back and it turned out he was a lawyer, and single. Well — divorced. My mother got this look on her face, and I knew exactly what she was thinking, because she has been trying to set me up for years.

notes.text: The time of the mother's discovery is not quite given: she bakes the cookies, then 'it turns out' — the reader is not told whether the mother learned it at the door or later. It is the hinge of the anecdote. I made the mother come back from the cookie call with the news, so the discovery belongs to her and the look on her face follows from something she just learned.
notes.after: She came back and it turned out he was a lawyer, and single. Well — divorced.

lessons: The chief difference is that your page states each thing in a short plain sentence, one fact at a time, while Twain runs the facts together in a long spoken line that piles up and then turns. I joined your separate sentences into cumulative sentences—"My mother baked them cakes right off, all in one whoosh, as the mother does—she wanted to find out everything about them: where they come from, what they done for work, whether they went to church"—so the anecdote flows like a man telling it aloud, and I let the big joke of "Well—divorced" sit short and flat at the end, as Twain would land it. Practise joining your short sentences with ", and" or a plain colon, and saving a very short sentence for the turn where the joke or the verdict lands.

reading.kind: story (a short personal anecdote in the present-tense narrator's voice, told to set up the mother's matchmaking)

outline.gist: A new family moved in next door last weekend; a huge truck, two little kids.
The dad seems nice; the mom is kind of standoffish.
The narrator's mother baked them cookies at once — to find out where they came from, what they did, whether they went to church.
The dad is a lawyer and single — 'well, divorced.'
The mother got a look; the narrator knew what she was thinking: she has been trying to set the narrator up for years.

plan.gist: A new family moved in next door last weekend; a huge truck and two little kids.
plan.why: Twain opens with the plain fact a neighbor would notice first, so the reader stands in the same yard and trusts the teller. State the small concrete things before any judgment; a big truck and two kids are what the eye catches, and they cost the reader nothing to hold.

plan.gist: The dad seems nice; the mom is kind of standoffish.
plan.why: Keep the writer's order: impressions before facts. Twain would make the reader complicit in the judging — report the looks plainly, then let the reader's own suspicion begin to work. A small doubt planted here pays off at the turn, and planting it before the fact, not after, is what makes a turn feel earned rather than announced.

plan.gist: Mother bakes cookies at once — to learn where they came from, what they did, whether they went to church.
plan.why: Twain loves a kindness with a motive inside it, so he would keep the cookies first and the interrogation second, in that order, letting the reader see the hook under the sugar. He would also keep the three questions as a list: a run of short specific questions reads funny and human where a summary ('to find out all about them') reads like a report. Concreteness is the argument here — the evidence that the mother is a campaigner with a system.

plan.gist: The dad is a lawyer and single — 'well, divorced.'
plan.why: Keep it exactly here, after the intelligence-gathering, because the mother's questions have been aimed at this answer all along; the reader arrives at it through her, and the plot and the joke are the same event. Twain would let the correction ('well, divorced') do the work of a comic deflation — the fact arrives, then the fact gets qualified — because a swift self-correction is how real speech, and Twain's speakers, land a joke.

plan.gist: The mother's look; the narrator knows what she is thinking: years of matchmaking.
plan.why: Twain keeps the close on the consequence and leaves the thought unsaid — the look does the talking, and the narrator's certainty tells the reader everything. End on the narrator's dry knowledge rather than on explanation, because a joke explained is a joke spent; the reader who has been let in will supply the rest, and supplying it is the pleasure.

sense.problem: Your first paragraph gives the new family a 'dad' and a 'mom'; your third says the dad is single — divorced. A household with a mother in it cannot also have a divorced father alone at its head, and the mother's matchmaking turns on his being free.
sense.quote: The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish. … It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.
sense.resolution: Keep every other sentence and make the 'mom' someone other than the dad's partner: the least change is to make her a relative or other adult in the house rather than the children's mother — e.g., 'his sister' (she moved in to help with the kids), or the kids' grandmother or a roommate. This removes the contradiction, leaves the dad single and divorced as the close needs him, and fits a divorced father with two kids and a household big enough for another adult. (If instead the 'mom' were meant as the ex-wife, she would not be living next door in his house, and the mother's cookie call would make no sense.)

sense.problem: The time of the mother's discovery is not quite given: she bakes the cookies, then 'it turns out' — the reader is not told whether the mother learned it at the door or later. Minor, but it is the hinge of the anecdote.
sense.quote: My mother baked them cookies right away. … It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single.
sense.resolution: One clause of least change: say the mother came back from the cookie call with the news ('By the time she came back, it turned out…'), so the discovery belongs to the mother and the look on her face follows from something she just learned.

faults.quote: baked them cakes right off
faults.why: The writer's cookies became cakes. This is an unreported change of fact, and it is not needed for the voice.

faults.quote: all in one whoosh, as the mother does
faults.why: This adds a mannerism and a generalization that were not in the draft. It is a flourish, not commentary the voice needs. 'Whoosh' is not Twain's diction, and 'as the mother does' is awkward.

faults.quote: She came back and it turned out he was a lawyer
faults.why: This invents an incident, the mother returning from a visit. The writer only said 'It turns out.' The note frames it as a sense mending, but the draft had no real fault there.

faults.quote: his sister, which helps with the two little ones
faults.why: The mending is plausible, but it invents a sister and a caregiving role. A more minimal mending would have been that the woman is simply an unnamed other adult, or the ex-wife visiting. 'Which helps' also breaks grammar for 'who'.

faults.quote: with a monstrous great truck
faults.why: This is a generic archaic gesture. The rewrite lacks Twain's real devices: deadpan understatement, a comic simile, a vernacular narrator with sustained rhythm. It reads as the original lightly retouched.

faults.quote: where they come from, what they done for work, whether they went to church
faults.why: The dialect is inconsistent. 'Come' and 'done' are Huck-style, but 'whether they went' and 'she has been trying' are standard. The tenses also drift between present 'come' and past 'went'.

faults.quote: seemed kind of offish
faults.why: This is a clipped hybrid of 'standoffish' and Twain-ish speech, and it is unclear. The note's claim that it stays 'standoffish' is not matched by the wording.

faults.quote: and I knew exactly what she was thinking, because she has been trying to set me up for years.
faults.why: This is plain modern phrasing, with no Twain flourish at the key close. It also changes the writer's separate sentences into a 'because' clause, which weakens the comic beat.

faults.quote: [liberty] Liberty taken: The deadpan generalization about the mother's way of doing things
faults.why: The note labels 'as the mother does' as deadpan, but it reads as a clumsy tag. The notes also do not mention the cookies-to-cakes change or the added 'monstrous great' and 'right off', so they are incomplete.

faults.quote: The chief difference is that your page states each thing in a short plain sentence
faults.why: The lesson claims long cumulative sentences, but the rewrite mostly keeps the writer's sentences. The advice is generic, and it quotes the 'whoosh' line as a model even though that line is a weak imitation.

faults.quote: Well — divorced.
faults.why: The deflation is kept, but it is not set up with Twain's builds. The structure outline promises that planting doubt gives the turn its weight, and the rewrite does not deliver on that.

judge.verdict: The rewrite mends the mom/divorced contradiction and reports it, but it does so by inventing a sister. It also changes cookies to cakes without saying so, adds a mother-returns incident, and offers only thin, inconsistent Twain flavor ('whoosh', mixed dialect). The notes and lesson are partly generic and oversell the changes.

Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon. If you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.

rewrite:
Boys:

The launch is moved from Tuesday to Thursday, and that's the news, and all of it. Legal has not signed off on the pricing page yet, and I don't want us shipping without it, which ain't comfortable.

Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday noon. And if you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.

rows.text: Boys:
The launch is moved from Tuesday to Thursday, and that's the news, and all of it. Legal has not signed off on the pricing page yet, and I don't want us shipping without it, which ain't comfortable.

notes.text: The voice's own verdict on shipping without the legal sign-off: it frames the writer's uneasiness without adding any new incident or feeling.
notes.after: which ain't comfortable

rows.text: Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday noon. And if you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.
Thanks, Sam.

lessons: The chief difference is that your note speaks in short, flat business telegraph; Twain's manner is a man talking it over, piling clauses with "and" until the point lands. I made the longest run of news into one cumulative sentence that ends on "which ain't comfortable"—the uneasiness stated deadpan at the close where it hits. Practise stitching your points with "and" so each one arrives with the weight of those before it, and keeping the plainest words ("moved", "sign off", "blocked") rather than the office words "update" and "shipping without it".

reading.kind: email (a team update with a reason, two requests, and a close).

outline.gist: “Hi team” — addresses the whole group.
The launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday.
Legal still hasn't signed off on the pricing page.
Sam doesn't want to ship without that sign-off.
Deck sections to be done by Wednesday noon.

outline.role: Request and deadline for speaking up
outline.gist: If blocked, say so today, not tomorrow.
“Thanks, Sam” — a sign-off with thanks.

plan.gist: “Hi team” as is.
plan.why: Twain keeps the plain greeting: an audience addressed directly listens; there is nothing to gain by dress.

plan.gist: The launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday.
plan.why: News first, so the reader knows at once what changed and reads everything after it as explanation; a reason placed before the news makes the reader guess what is being explained.

plan.gist: Legal still hasn't signed off on the pricing page.
plan.why: The cause follows the effect, which is how a reader checks an announcement; and “still” carries the whole history of waiting in one word, so no extra sentences are needed to work up to it.

plan.gist: Sam doesn't want to ship without the sign-off.
plan.why: A decision with a stated owner reads as a decision, not an accident; the reader sees who chose and can trust the date. Twain always lets the reader see whose judgment they are following.

plan.gist: Deck sections done by Wednesday noon.
plan.why: The request comes after the reason, so it looks like a consequence rather than an order; and it is put as one plain deadline with one clock, which is what a reader acts on.

plan.gist: If blocked, say so today, not tomorrow.
plan.why: This is the one place Twain would sharpen the contrast, because “today, not tomorrow” is the whole point of the sentence and the reader must not miss that the writer is asking for bad news early. A short paired contrast is the cheapest way to make it stick.

plan.gist: “Thanks, Sam.”
plan.why: Twain ends short. After the ask, more words only dilute it; the sign-off with thanks leaves the reader with the request and a person behind it.

faults.quote: which ain't comfortable
faults.why: Adds a new feeling (discomfort) the writer never expressed; the writer said only 'I don't want us shipping without it.' Its placement also makes 'which' ambiguous: does it mean the lack of sign-off or shipping?

faults.quote: Boys:
faults.why: Changes 'Hi team' to 'Boys', which assumes a gendered, all-male audience and alters the addressee. The writer addressed a mixed team.

faults.quote: and that's the news, and all of it
faults.why: Adds a flourish not in the original; the writer's 'Quick update' is replaced by an invented assertion, which is filler rather than a change in meaning.

faults.quote: Thanks, Sam.
faults.why: The line is collapsed to one line, losing the email's signature layout. Minor.

faults.quote: Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday noon. And if you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.
faults.why: These sentences are left almost verbatim in modern office English, with 'Please' and 'blocked', so half the piece is not Twain at all. There is no wit, no concrete image, no understatement beyond one grafted phrase.

faults.quote: ain't comfortable
faults.why: A single dialect tag in an otherwise modern register reads as costume; Twain's humor comes from deadpan exaggeration or concrete comparison, not just 'ain't'.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: The voice's own verdict on shipping without the legal sign-off: it frames the writer's uneasiness without adding any new incident or feeling.
faults.why: Claims no new feeling was added, but 'ain't comfortable' is an added feeling/verdict. The notes also leave paragraphs 1, 3 and 4 unannotated even though 'Boys:' and 'and that's the news, and all of it' were changes.

faults.quote: (no notes)
faults.why: Changes in the greeting and first sentence (Hi team→Boys, added 'that's the news') go unreported; no moves are named with sources.

faults.quote: Practise stitching your points with "and" so each one arrives with the weight of those before it
faults.why: Weak, generic advice that the rewrite barely demonstrates (only one 'and' chain). It also advises against 'shipping without it' as an office word, though the rewrite keeps that phrase. The how_it_is_built section says Twain keeps 'Hi team', contradicting the rewrite's 'Boys:'.

faults.quote: Boys:
faults.why: The outline said the greeting stays as is, but the rewrite changed it, an inconsistency between outline and output. Order is otherwise kept, though the 'Legal... I don't want us shipping' reason pairing is merged into one sentence with the added aside.

judge.verdict: The rewrite is almost the original with 'Boys', 'ain't comfortable' and a filler clause bolted on. It adds a feeling and a gendered address, fails to sound like Twain, and the notes misreport what was changed.

Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends. Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

We should try it this summer.
rewrite:
The town ought to shut Main Street against wagons and horses on a Saturday and a Sunday. A body can scarce turn around down there of a day, what with the carriages crammed every which way, and the sidewalks so narrow a baby-wagon can't get past without a shove into the gutter. There's towns that has tried it, and their shops do a better trade than they ever did before.

Some of the business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But the customers will get used to the walk, for the most part they walk from the carriage-house anyway.

We might try it this summer, and see.

rows.text: The town ought to shut Main Street against wagons and horses on a Saturday and a Sunday. A body can scarce turn around down there of a day, what with the carriages crammed every which way, and the sidewalks so narrow a baby-wagon can't get past without a shove into the gutter. There's towns that has tried it, and their shops do a better trade than they ever did before.

notes.text: The voice frames the narrow sidewalks in the teller's own plain words, keeping to what the writer says but showing it instead of naming it.
notes.after: a body can scarce turn around

rows.text: Some of the business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But the customers will get used to the walk, for the most part they walk from the carriage-house anyway.

notes.text: The answer to the owners' objection mixes two subjects: 'they'll get used to it' points at the business owners, while 'most people walk from the garage anyway' is about customers. I named each subject plainly: the customers are the ones who will get used to the walk, and most people already walk from the garage. That answers the owners' objection about customers' arriving without adding any new fact.
notes.after: But the customers will get used to the walk, for the most part they walk from the carriage-house anyway.

rows.text: We might try it this summer, and see.

lessons: Your passage names the plan and never shows the street; Twain's narrator lets us see the carriage crammed sideways and the baby-wagon shoved into the gutter, and the verdict lands harder because he never says 'nightmare'—he just shows it, deadpan. Practise that: where you wrote 'Parking downtown is a nightmare,' I wrote 'a body can scarce turn around down there of a day,' and piled the clauses with 'and' the way Huck does until the joke arrives at the end, unexplained. And instead of 'Honestly,' which argues, I let the voice confide 'for the most part,' which sounds like a man reasoning it out beside you, so the reader takes the point as his own.

reading.kind: argument (a short opinion piece proposing a town policy)

outline.gist: Main Street should be closed to cars on weekends.
Parking downtown is a nightmare; sidewalks are too narrow for strollers.
Other towns did it and their shops are doing better than ever.
Some owners will say customers can't get to them.
People will get used to it; most walk from the garage anyway.
Try it this summer.

plan.gist: Close Main Street to cars on weekends.
plan.why: Twain leads with the proposal in one blunt sentence, so the reader knows what is being asked and can measure every later reason against it; a claim buried under complaints reads as grumbling, while a claim stated first reads as a proposition to be judged.

plan.gist: Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks can't hold a stroller.
plan.why: He starts from what the reader has felt in his own legs and temper, not from statistics; a shared annoyance admitted plainly is the cheapest kind of agreement, and it buys the reader's attention for the argument still to come. He would keep the writer's order here, since the complaint is the natural doorway to the cure.

plan.gist: Other towns have done it and their shops are doing better than ever.
plan.why: He follows the felt trouble with the witnessed proof, because an anxious reader asks 'does it work?' before 'is it right?'; a precedent from towns like ours answers that question before it can be raised as an objection, and it is the writer's own order kept, since the example already sits exactly where it does the most good.

plan.gist: Some owners will say customers can't get to them.
plan.why: Twain gives the other side its best words in its own mouth, even lending it a little sympathy, because an objection answered before it is fairly stated only convinces the reader that the writer is hiding something; letting the owner speak in his own voice makes the answer look like a fair win rather than a trick.

plan.gist: Most people walk from the garage anyway, and habits adjust.
plan.why: He answers the owners' fear with the plain fact of how people already get downtown, then grants that adjusting takes time — the order matters: the fact first settles the question of whether customers can reach the shops at all, and the concession about getting used to it then costs nothing. This is where the writer's own answer needs one added link: say plainly that the walk from the garage is short and that the closed street is what people will be walking to, so 'they'll get used to it' is tied to the same people the objection is about.

plan.gist: Try it this summer.
plan.why: Twain ends small on purpose — a trial for one season is a request no fair-minded reader can refuse, and refusing to demand permanence removes the last fear the owner had; a modest close also leaves the reader feeling that the burden of proof has shifted, which is exactly what a proposal wants when the meeting ends.

sense.problem: The answer to the owners' objection mixes two subjects: 'they'll get used to it' grammatically points at the business owners, while 'most people walk from the garage anyway' is about customers. The reader cannot tell whether habits of owners, of customers, or of parking are what must change, so the objection is never quite answered.
sense.quote: Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.
sense.resolution: Name the subject in each sentence, with the least change: 'Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But most people already walk from the garage anyway, and customers will get used to the short walk.' This keeps the writer's words and order, but makes clear that the customers are the ones who adjust, which is what the owners' objection actually concerns. Do not substitute a new fact (such as the length of the walk) unless the writer supplies it; if it is not true that the garage is near, say instead only that customers will get used to the walk.

sense.problem: No true echo. The nearest scene of Twain's is the Connecticut Yankee dropping a scheme onto a town that did not ask for it, but that scene turns on a modern man forcing improvements on the past; this passage merely proposes a trial to the town's own people, and takes nothing from the scene that its own argument does not already have.
sense.quote: We should try it this summer.
sense.resolution: No borrowing needed. If the rewrite wants a handle, the Yankee's habit of measuring a scheme by what it plainly saves people — time, temper, shoe leather — is the only thing worth carrying over, and the passage's 'try it this summer' already does that work.

faults.quote: against wagons and horses
faults.why: The writer said 'cars'. The rewrite swaps in wagons and horses, and later 'carriages'. This relocates the setting to the 1800s and alters the facts, and the town's cars become something else.

faults.quote: the carriages crammed every which way
faults.why: The writer's problem is parking ('Parking downtown is a nightmare'). Carriages 'crammed every which way' is a traffic image, not a parking one, and the specific complaint about parking is lost.

faults.quote: without a shove into the gutter
faults.why: This invents an incident (a baby-wagon shoved into the gutter) that the writer never mentioned. The writer only said the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers.

faults.quote: from the carriage-house anyway
faults.why: The writer's 'garage' becomes a 'carriage-house'. This changes the fact from a parking garage to a private building and muddles the argument that people already walk from public parking.

faults.quote: Saturday and a Sunday
faults.why: 'Weekends' is narrowed slightly. This is minor but it is a change.

faults.quote: and see
faults.why: This adds a hedge, 'and see'. It softens the writer's flat 'We should try it' into 'might', which lowers the force of the call to action.

faults.quote: But the customers will get used to the walk, for the most part they walk from the carriage-house anyway.
faults.why: The fault was a mixed subject (owners versus customers). The rewrite fixes it, but 'the walk' makes the claim unclear, and the comma splice makes 'for the most part' read as if it hedges the first clause. The note says the sense is mended, but the answer remains weak, and the how_it_is_built advice (the closed street is what people will be walking to) was not applied.

faults.quote: There's towns that has tried it
faults.why: This is an ungrammatical dialect that goes past Twain's narrator voice into Huck-style grammar, then clashes with the 'ought to shut' formality of the opening. The register is inconsistent.

faults.quote: A body can scarce turn around down there of a day
faults.why: A stock folksy phrase pile-up. It has some Twain flavor but little of his actual comic engine: there is no exaggeration, no deadpan turn, no ironic reversal. The rest is plain.

faults.quote: A body can scarce turn around down there of a day
faults.why: 'Of a day' is awkward as a time marker here, and the sentence loses the writer's point about weekends.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: The voice frames the narrow sidewalks in the teller's own plain words, keeping to what the writer says but showing it instead of naming it.
faults.why: The note understates the changes. It does not report the cars-to-wagons substitution, the invented gutter shove, or the garage-to-carriage-house change. It claims 'keeping to what the writer says' when new content was added.

faults.quote: That answers the owners' objection about customers' arriving without adding any new fact.
faults.why: The note claims no new fact was added, but 'carriage-house' changes a fact. There are no notes on paragraph 3 or on moves such as the dialect.

faults.quote: I wrote 'a body can scarce turn around down there of a day,' and piled the clauses with 'and' the way Huck does until the joke arrives at the end, unexplained.
faults.why: The lesson claims a technique (a pile-up that ends in a joke) that the text does not execute, and it attributes the style to Huck rather than to Twain's own narrator. It also praises 'for the most part' as confiding when it is a weak hedge, and the lesson never mentions the era shift.

faults.quote: We might try it this summer, and see.
faults.why: The order is kept, but the objection is not stated at full strength as the outline recommends, and the answer is not rebuilt. The close is weaker than the writer's.

judge.verdict: The rewrite shifts the setting from cars to carriages and wagons, invents a gutter incident, and softens the close. It uses a patchy dialect that is not much like Twain's. The notes and lesson do not honestly report these changes.

I know it's risky and clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and see.

I judge we ought to give over working six days and put up with four, for the people are wore out, and our best engineer has up and quit. There's studies that show the work don't fall off none—it stays where it was, or maybe up, and never down. It would help with the hiring too, I reckon.

I know it's risky, and the clients might not take to it; but we could try it for three months and see how it goes.

notes.after: It would help with the hiring too, I reckon.

notes.text: The voice gives the proposal as the narrator's own settled judgment, which the passage implies by 'I think we should'; 'judge' is the teller's plain confidence.
notes.after: I judge we ought to

notes.text: The passage says stays the same or goes up; the voice stretches it into a confident aside that the worst case is the work keeps steady, framing the argument deadpan.
notes.after: maybe up, and never down

rows.text: I know it's risky, and the clients might not take to it; but we could try it for three months and see how it goes.

lessons: Your draft is clean and airless—ten plain words to a sentence, no commas, no voice. Twain's manner is a man talking: \"I judge we ought to give over working six days and put up with four\" gives the proposal a teller's confidence, and the cumulative chain \"it stays where it was, or maybe up, and never down\" lets the argument build and then land its joke flat, without explaining. reading.kind: argument (a short proposal memo in miniature)

outline.gist: We should switch to a four-day week.
Burnout; the best engineer just quit; studies show productivity holds or rises; it would help hiring.
It is risky and clients might not like it.
Try it for three months and see.

faults.quote: give over working six days and put up with four
faults.why: The writer never mentions six days. A current six-day week is an invented fact. The original proposes only to switch to a four-day week.

faults.quote: it stays where it was, or maybe up, and never down
faults.why: The writer said productivity 'stays the same or goes up.' Adding 'never down' and 'maybe' shifts the degree of certainty and adds an assertion.

faults.quote: the work don't fall off none
faults.why: 'The work' is not 'productivity' in the studies. It also bends the meaning slightly, and the double negative is a Huck Finn dialect that Twain's essayistic voice would not use for a workplace memo.

faults.quote: the people are wore out, and our best engineer has up and quit
faults.why: This is Huck's rural dialect, not the voice of Twain as a speaker or essayist. It is a mix of 'wore out', 'up and quit', and 'There's studies', and it reads as costume. Twain's wit is missing: no irony, no exaggeration, no comic comparison.

faults.quote: I judge we ought to
faults.why: 'I judge' is a Huck-type idiom, and the sentence has none of Twain's deadpan comic turn. The rewrite is a plain paraphrase in dialect.

faults.quote: There's studies that show the work don't fall off none—it stays where it was
faults.why: The mix of dialect grammar with an em-dash restatement is clumsy. The 'none' and 'don't' feel pasted on.

faults.quote: put up with four

yours:
When Dana cancelled our dinner I wasn't upset at all. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.
rewrite:
When Dana put off our dinner I wasn't troubled a bit, and I don't mind saying it. I was glad of it, and that's the plain truth—I'd been dreading it all week, and I wasn't proud of dreading it, and that's a fact.

I told her it was all right, and we'd take it up another time, which was a comfort to her no doubt. But I don't reckon we ever will.

lessons: The chief difference is that your passage states its feelings flatly, one short sentence at a time, while Twain's narrator talks them out, piling up clauses and letting the honest admission arrive at the end of the run. You used "I was relieved" as a bare report; I made it a cumulative sentence ("I was glad of it, and that's the plain truth—I'd been dreading it all week...") so the confession lands last and unexplained. Practise ending your long "and... and..." sentences on the quiet verdict—"I don't reckon we ever will"—so the deadpan undercut does the work a statement cannot.

reading.kind: story (a very short first-person anecdote); near enough to a letter in its direct address, but it is told, not sent.

outline.gist: Dana cancelled dinner; the narrator felt not upset but relieved
The dread had run all week; the narrator is not proud of it
The narrator told Dana it was fine and they'd do it another time
The narrator doubts there will be another time

plan.gist: Dana cancelled dinner; the narrator was not upset but relieved — the plain claim first, before any apology
plan.why: Twain states the bald, slightly shameful truth flat and early, so the reader is won by candor before there is any chance to moralize; a confession delayed reads as a defense.

plan.gist: The dread had been building all week; the narrator is not proud of it
plan.why: The admission of dread gives the relief a cause, so the feeling is evidence rather than mere assertion; adding the ‘not proud’ keeps the narrator honest and lets the reader side with him, the way Huck wins sympathy by owning his worst thoughts.

plan.gist: The narrator told Dana it was fine and they'd do it another time — the polite lie set beside the private truth
plan.why: Putting the spoken words right after the private ones lets the reader measure the gap without the narrator explaining it; the contrast does the work, and a stated contrast is half as funny as an enacted one.

plan.gist: A flat, short doubt that there will be another time
plan.why: The close lands hardest short and dry; the brevity lets the reader supply the rueful laugh, which is the point of the piece. A long close would explain away the very thing that makes it sting.

faults.quote: which was a comfort to her no doubt
faults.why: This adds a new claim about Dana's reaction that the writer never made. It is commentary, but it invents Dana's feelings and slightly shifts the writer's guilt into sarcasm.

faults.quote: and I don't mind saying it
faults.why: This changes the writer's shame ('I'm not proud of that') into a casual, unashamed tone, and it contradicts the later 'wasn't proud'. The feeling is weakened.

faults.quote: I wasn't proud of dreading it
faults.why: The writer was not proud of being relieved and of the dread. Here the shame attaches only to the dreading, which is a slight shift. The repeated 'and that's a fact' also adds filler.

faults.quote: and that's the plain truth—I'd been dreading it all week, and I wasn't proud of dreading it, and that's a fact.
faults.why: 'Plain truth' and 'that's a fact' are doubled, stacked tags. They read as pastiche rather than Twain's actual dry understatement, and the repetition blunts the deadpan.

faults.quote: I wasn't troubled a bit
faults.why: This is generic folksy phrasing. It is not specific Twain, and the passage has no concrete image or comic exaggeration.

faults.quote: But I don't reckon we ever will.
faults.why: 'ever' strengthens the writer's tentative 'I don't think we will'. 'Reckon' is a Huck-ish dialect word that clashes with the more narrator-polished register elsewhere.

faults.quote: cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 18, ¶ 1
faults.why: The citations look unverified and loosely apt. Ch. 8 ¶ 4 is not a known source for an aside of this kind. The notes also call the closing 'the narrator's aside' when the aside is really the inserted 'comfort to her' clause.

faults.quote: The writer's bare doubt is said in the narrator's own idiom, a quiet undercutting of the polite lie
faults.why: The note describes the doubt sentence but does not report the added 'comfort to her no doubt' clause as an addition. It is labelled only as an aside, so the writer is not told that new content was introduced.

faults.quote: so the confession lands last and unexplained
faults.why: The lesson claims the confession lands last, but in the rewrite it ends with 'that's a fact', which is the opposite of the dry, short close the outline praises. The advice contradicts the built structure and gives little transferable guidance.

faults.quote: I wasn't proud of dreading it, and that's a fact.
faults.why: The outline says the confession should be flat and brief, with a short dry close. The rewrite pads the first paragraph and puts the deadpan into an added sarcastic clause, not an enacted contrast.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the basic facts and the direction of feeling. But it adds an invented comment about Dana's comfort, softens the shame, and leans on stacked folksy tags that read as costume. The notes are thin, with doubtful citations and an unreported addition, and the lesson contradicts what the rewrite does.
